articles.title: Justiça revoga mandado de prisão de líder separatista catalão, que pode voltar à Espanha nove anos após ter deixado país | G1
articles.standfirst: Carles Puigdemont deixou país da península ibérica após uma tentativa fracassada de independência. Além dele, foram revogados mandados para os ex-conselheiros Antoni Comín e Lluís Puig.
articles.summary:
Carles Puigdemont deixou país da península ibérica após uma tentativa fracassada de independência. 
Além dele, foram revogados mandados para os ex-conselheiros Antoni Comín e Lluís Puig.
articles.body:
Carles Puigdemont, líder separatista catalão teve mandado de prisão revogado pela justiça espanhola. — Foto: Nacho Doce/Reuters

O Supremo Tribunal espanhol anunciou, nesta terça-feira (6), que revogou a ordem de prisão contra o líder independentista catalão Carles Puigdemont, que agora poderá retornar à Espanha quase nove anos após ter partido depois da tentativa fracassada de secessão.

"O magistrado da Sala Penal do Supremo, Pablo Llarena, emitiu hoje uma decisão revogando, com efeito imediato e até nova resolução judicial expressa, as ordens nacionais de busca, captura e prisão do ex-presidente da Generalitat da Catalunha, Carles Puigdemont, e dos ex-conselheiros Antoni Comín e Lluís Puig", informou o tribunal em comunicado.

A decisão foi divulgada pouco depois de o Tribunal Constitucional validar a aplicação da lei de anistia, aprovada há dois anos pelo Parlamento espanhol, também ao crime de peculato.

Logo em seguida, o presidente do governo espanhol, Pedro Sánchez, celebrou a notícia, afirmando que ela permite à Catalunha "olhar para o futuro".

"Celebramos o fato de que, com isso, também ajudamos a sociedade catalã, como ela vinha reivindicando durante todo esse tempo", declarou em entrevista coletiva.

articles.title: Mumbai's Kalu river throws up hundreds of dead fish, activist blames Ulhasnagar effluent surge
articles.summary: MUMBAI: The sun rose on the Kalu as it did every other day. But on Sunday, along with it rose fish - hundreds, stippling the waters in grisly pointillism.
articles.body: MUMBAI: The sun rose on the Kalu as it did every other day. But on Sunday, along with it rose fish - hundreds, stippling the waters in grisly pointillism. Avinash Harad, an environmental activist who had led a group of six researchers on a biodiversity survey to a site on the river - the ferry crossing at Atali and Nandkar, villages on either side of the Kalu - said hundreds of fish had floated to the surface, dead or dying."The fish died because of untreated effluents from upstream dyeing units in Ulhasnagar that flowed into the Kalu at high tide," Harad said.He said the sluice gates of the KT Dam in Titwala are opened during the rains, bringing a surge of water during high tide that conveys factory discharge downstream. "The fish - mostly catfish and tilapia - died along at least 1 km of the Kalu, just before it meets the Ulhas river."On Sunday morning, Khandu Koli, a fisherman from Nandkar Koliwada in Bhiwandi taluka, was out on the river with 35-40 fishers from Atali and Nandkar, scooping fish out in handheld nets. Koli, whose own family netted 55 kg, said the phenomenon is not uncommon. "But we don't fish when the water turns black," he said.The catch was sold, with a small portion reserved for the fishers' own consumption.Jehu Nadar, a zoologist in the survey group, said prawns had surfaced alongside the fish. Both were dead by 10am.Nadar said the waters were dark green. The team collected samples and found many parameters off the charts: total dissolved solids (TDS) at Atali measured 210 parts per million (ppm), dissolved oxygen (DO) fell to 1.28 mg/L - far below the optimal 6-8 mg/L that aquatic life needs to survive. Upstream at Gurawali Bridge in Titwala , by contrast, TDS was 95.2 ppm and DO 5.53 mg/L."Mystus catfish can tolerate very poor water quality, and tilapia are notoriously tough. If they are turning up dead, the water has reached an absolute zero-survival threshold," Nadar said.The friend of a local fisher who accompanied the group forewarned them of the die-off on Saturday. "He got wind that effluents had been discharged upstream," Nadar said. articles.title: What is the future for our medium-sized shopping centres?
articles.summary: In the internet age, medium-sized retail hubs are looking for new ways to survive and thrive.
articles.body:
The Brunel Centre was once a thriving retail destination, attracting shoppers from far and wide.

"It was incredible," says town councillor Keith Ely, who remembers its opening in Bletchley, Buckinghamshire, in 1973.

Back then, centre:MK, a large destination shopping centre four miles away in Milton Keynes, did not exist, and the Brunel was quite the draw.

Now, like many other medium-sized shopping centres, it is struggling.

Vacant units and graffiti-daubed shutters dominate, and it has just one store left.

That remaining shop, a Boots Opticians, is set to close later this month ahead of the centre's planned demolition next year .

But Ely, 87, is not upset to see the Brunel make way for flats and a health centre, with only some retail space.

"It is a sad old building, isn't it?" he says. "There is no nostalgia from me."

In the Grafton Centre, Cambridge, it is a similar story, with shuttered units, a large empty former Debenhams department store and a permanently closed cinema.

There are long-term plans for a redevelopment to include retail but also a life science centre.

This may work in Cambridge, a global leader in life sciences, but it is not an option in much of the country.

So, in the age of online shopping, what lies ahead for these medium-sized malls?

"There are too many in the UK and many don't have a future," is the stark assessment of Subjit Jassy, a director at Pioneer Group, which owns the centre.

"The old model of retailers expanding to improve turnover has now disappeared because of the internet."

Analysis by commercial property firm CBRE found that while the vacancy rate across UK shopping centres in the second quarter of this year was 16%, it was "significantly lower" at major centres.

Meanwhile, research by estate agents Savills found between April and June 2026 almost 73% of consumer spending in shopping centres was in the biggest sites, with less than 18% in secondary, or medium-sized centres.

"It is not just that shopping centres have one destiny; they really don't," says Dr Kardi Somerfield, a lecturer in marketing at the University of Northampton.

Some destination shopping centres are running at "almost 100% occupancy", she adds.

Back at the Brunel, Labour's Ed Hume, responsible for housing at Milton Keynes City Council, says: "We do need shops.

"The change here is about making sure we have a town centre that is much more open."

The hope is that more town centre homes will increase the number of people to use local businesses.

Similar plans in Norwich will see the Anglia Square development primarily replaced by housing.

But there are other options rather than just tearing a centre down.

Market Walk in Northampton is t o become a leisure and entertainment space .

"Other shopping centres have a really important purpose as a community hub," says Somerfield, outlining another potential use.

This is what management are trying to achieve at another site that opened in the 1970s: Weston Favell, on the eastern edge of Northampton.

Footfall – the number of customers entering the building – has increased every year since the pandemic, says centre manager Kevin Legg.

"Other shopping centres are trying to emulate and create what we've got."

What they have got is a mix of a large supermarket, a number of big national brands and smaller independent businesses, as well as other community facilities.

Not far from the library inside the centre is a church. It is currently being used by Silhouette Youth Theatre, a charity that aims to make the arts more accessible.

Next year it plans to create a 250-seat theatre inside part of a former Wilko store.

George Grande, voice lead at Silhouette, says being located in a shopping centre means more people can easily arrive by public transport and gives the group more visibility.

"We've had it before where people are like 'Oh, what's this? We don't know what this is.'

"That is how we can get other people to join us."

articles.title: Germany is turning abandoned coal mines into 23 lakes; the former mining landscape is becoming Europe's largest artificial wetland
articles.summary: In eastern Germany, enormous pits carved into the landscape by decades of lignite mining are being transformed into a vast network of lakes, wetlands and
articles.body: In eastern Germany, enormous pits carved into the landscape by decades of lignite mining are being transformed into a vast network of lakes, wetlands and restored land. The Lusatian Lakeland, spread across Brandenburg and Saxony between Berlin and Dresden, is being created by flooding former open-cast mines and reshaping their surroundings. The tourist destination now comprises 23 post-mining lakes covering about 14,000 hectares of water. The transformation began with Lake Senftenberg in 1967 and has continued for decades, turning one of Germany's major coal-producing regions into a new water landscape. The project combines environmental restoration with tourism, recreation and long-term rehabilitation of land heavily altered by mining.Germany transforms coal pits to a giant lake landscapeLusatia was one of Germany's major lignite-mining regions, and open-cast extraction left huge excavated areas after the coal was removed. The first major step towards their transformation began in 1967, when the former Niemtsch open-cast mine started filling to create Lake Senftenberg. Flooding was completed in 1972, and the lake opened for public use the following year. Since then, numerous other mine pits have been flooded, creating what regional authorities describe as Europe's largest artificial water landscape. The process has involved both groundwater and water brought in from rivers and other sources. According to mining-rehabilitation company LMBV, the rapid flooding of some mine voids was necessary because the enormous quantities of material removed during mining left large depressions that could not simply be restored to their original form.A network of 23 post-mining lakesThe Lusatian Lakeland is not a single giant lake but a collection of former mining sites that are gradually being integrated into a connected water landscape. LMBV identifies 23 post-mining lakes within the tourist destination, with a combined water surface of around 14,000 hectares. Five of the most prominent are Senftenberger See, Geierswalder See, Partwitzer See, Sedlitzer See and Großräschener See. Their transformation has taken place over different periods, with Senftenberger See being the oldest of the group and Sedlitzer See among the most recent to reach its target level. In 2025, Sedlitzer See reached its planned water level, marking a major stage in the creation of the lake network. At about 1,400 hectares, it has become the largest recreational lake in the Lusatian region.Five lakes now form a connected waterwayThe transformation is extending beyond the creation of individual lakes. Canals are being constructed to connect several of the former mining pits, allowing boats to move between lakes that were once separated by mining infrastructure and spoil heaps. On June 29, 2026, five major lakes were officially connected through navigable waterways, creating a continuous water area of roughly 5,100 hectares. The network includes Senftenberger See, Geierswalder See, Partwitzer See, Sedlitzer See and Großräschener See. LMBV says the wider plan involves 13 navigable canals, of which four have been completed, while others are under construction or in planning. The new connections are intended to support boating and passenger shipping while creating a unified tourism destination from landscapes that were once dominated by mining.Nature is returning around the former minesThe creation of lakes is only one part of the region's environmental transformation. Mining rehabilitation has also involved stabilising former mine slopes, restoring land and allowing new vegetation to establish across areas that were previously heavily disturbed. Young forests are growing on former spoil heaps, while grasslands, wetlands and other habitats are emerging around the newly created water bodies. The changing landscape is therefore not simply an exercise in filling holes with water, but a long-term effort to establish a functioning post-mining environment. The scale of the intervention is considerable: LMBV says about 15,000 hectares of water surface has already emerged in the Lusatian Lakeland, while additional post-mining lakes continue to be developed elsewhere in Germany's former mining regions.A new future for a former coal regionThe lakes are also changing the economic identity of Lusatia. Beaches, marinas, cycling routes, campsites and water-sports facilities are being developed alongside the restored landscape, while parts of the region's industrial history remain visible through mining heritage sites and visitor attractions. The transformation is particularly significant because it is taking place in an area whose landscape and economy were shaped for generations by lignite extraction. The result is a new regional identity built around water, recreation and nature while retaining links to the industrial past. Regional authorities describe the Lusatian Lakeland as Germany's fourth-largest lake district and Europe's largest artificial water landscape. What began with the flooding of a single former mine in 1967 has consequently grown into a decades-long landscape transformation involving two dozen lakes, interconnected waterways and thousands of hectares of reclaimed land.You use AI every day. articles.title: NYPD detective released from hospital after being stabbed multiple times in Bronx
articles.summary: New York City Police Department Detective Jose Mercedes walked out of Jacobi Medical Center after being stabbed multiple times in a Bronx robbery.
articles.body: A New York City Police Department detective was released from the hospital after he was stabbed multiple times during a robbery in the Bronx last week, according to officials. Detective Jose Mercedes was wheeled out of Jacobi Medical Center in Morris Park on Monday before standing up in front of a group of clapping officers. "Today, in another incredible feat of strength and determination, Detective Mercedes got up from his wheelchair and walked out of Jacobi Medical Center on his own two feet. Hundreds of members of the NYPD were there to cheer their brother on," Police Commissioner Jessica Tisch said on X. NYPD DETECTIVE, CHILDREN SHOT IN SEPARATE BROOKLYN SHOOTINGS OVER HOLIDAY WEEKEND "The entire department stands behind Detective Mercedes as he continues his recovery. And the greatest detectives in the world will relentlessly pursue those responsible for this crime," she added. Mercedes was off-duty when two suspects on an e-bike attempted to snatch his gold chain as he was clearing out the trunk of his car in the Norwood neighborhood on Friday afternoon, according to officials. WATCH: E-BIKE TEEN TAKEOVER SWARMS DOWNTOWN CITY STREETS BLOCKING TRAFFIC, LEADING TO CHARGES The detective attempted to fight back, but he was stabbed and slashed seven times during the struggle before the assailants fled. Authorities said the confrontation began when the men attempted to steal his gold chain. Mercedes then pursued the fleeing attackers on foot for about two blocks before collapsing near East 206th Street and Rochambeau Avenue. "Despite his serious injuries, Detective Mercedes chased after his attackers on foot," Tisch said. "I visited the detective and his family at Jacobi Hospital with Police Commissioner Tisch," the mayor said on Friday. "I am hoping for his quick and complete recovery." The two attackers remain at large, police said on Monday.

articles.title: In 1994, a golfer paid $5 for a green jacket at a Toronto thrift store; it was later confirmed as an authentic 1950s Augusta National club jacket, and it sold at auction in 2017 for $139,349
articles.summary: A golfer was browsing through a Toronto thrift store when he came across a green jacket. The item looked interesting, and he knew this was an unusual find.
articles.body: A golfer was browsing through a Toronto thrift store when he came across a green jacket. The item looked interesting, and he knew this was an unusual find. It was priced at $5, so he bought it anyway.More than two decades later, the same jacket was sold for $139,349 at auction after Augusta National Golf Club confirmed that it was an authentic club jacket dating to the 1950s, Global News reported.The jacket was later known as a ‘thrift-store Masters jacket’, an unusual piece of golf memorabilia offered by Green Jacket Auctions in 2017.A $5 findAn avid golfer and a member of the Canadian media discovered the jacket while browsing through a Toronto second-hand shop in 1994. He recognised the Augusta National branding and decided to buy it. He paid just $5 for the jacket, unaware of just how valuable it could eventually become. At the time, the jacket had no name, so its history remained unclear. But a tag on the jacket indicated that it dated to the 1950s. The jacket was later sold to a British golf journalist, who kept it for years before it eventually appeared at auction.Augusta National identifies the jacketThe green jacket turned out to be an authentic Augusta National club jacket. Augusta National confirmed its authenticity. The green jacket is one of the most recognisable symbols in golf, and it is closely associated with Augusta National and the Masters Tournament.Members of the Georgia club wear these distinctive jackets, and the Masters winner traditionally receives one after winning the tournament. So they finalised that this jacket was a club member's jacket, not one awarded to a Masters champion.During the auction, everything about the jacket, from its age and link to Augusta National to its unusual journey from a Toronto thrift store, made it a fascinating piece of golf memorabilia.$5 jacket auctioned for $139,349During the Spring 2017 golf-memorabilia sale, Green Jacket Auctions included this jacket. The auction featured a collection of historically significant Masters items.The bidding for this jacket began at $5,000 and attracted 34 bids before closing at $139,349.“We are blown away by the interest in golf memorabilia right now. The golf-collecting hobby has never been so strong. Yet, when you look at golf memorabilia compared to baseball and other sports, golf is selling at a relative bargain. Surely because of this we’re starting to see ‘smart’ money enter the hobby. Wealthy New Yorkers and international buyers who want the very best pieces are willing to pay what are record prices for the golf hobby because they believe that there is still a great deal of upside with the top pieces of memorabilia,” Ryan Carey, an attorney who is one of the two principals at Green Jacket Auctions, which was established in 2006, told Golf Digest.The buyer was a private collector from the United States. Green Jacket Auctions did not disclose the person's identity.For the person who found the jacket at the thrift store, this sale was nothing less than a lottery. A jacket bought for $5 had become a six-figure collector's item.Despite being sold for $139,349, this green jacket was far from the most expensive green jacket ever sold. Yes, you read that right. Back in 2013, a green jacket reportedly belonging to Horton Smith, who won the first Masters Tournament in 1934 and won again in 1936, was sold for $682,229. This 2017 sale, however, showed how much collectors were willing to pay for rare pieces of Masters history.You use AI every day. Now get your AI Quotient. Take the AIQ test.

articles.title: Trump approves firing squad execution for Fort Hood attacker Nidal Hasan
articles.summary: Pentagon confirms execution order for Nidal Hasan, convicted of killing 13 in Fort Hood shooting in 2009.
articles.body:
United States President Donald Trump has ordered the use of a firing squad in the execution of a former army psychiatrist who killed 13 people in a mass shooting at Fort Hood, Texas, in 2009, the Pentagon spokesman has said.

Nidal Hasan, a US citizen of Palestinian descent, would be the first US soldier to be executed by the US military in more than 60 years.

Hasan will be killed by a firing squad under the recommendation of Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth and the approval of the president, Pentagon spokesperson Sean Parnell said in a statement on X on Monday.

The Army secretary will decide a time and place for the execution, he said.

“Judgement day for Hasan has finally come,” Parnell wrote.

Hasan was sentenced to death in August 2013 after a military jury found him guilty of 45 counts of premeditated murder and attempted murder for shooting a handgun in a medical facility at the Texas military base.

The attack killed 12 unarmed active-duty soldiers and a retired serviceman, and wounded 32 others.

Police arrested him at the scene, where he was shot and left partially paralysed.

The shooting took place weeks before Hasan was set to be deployed to Afghanistan.

He said during his court-martial that the shooting was an effort to stop the soldiers from going to Afghanistan and killing his fellow Muslims, and made almost no effort to defend himself.

The Trump administration added death by firing squad as an appropriate method of execution in April, along with gas asphyxiation and electrocution.

Military executions are extremely rare in the US and can only be approved by the president under the Uniform Code of Military Justice. If the order is carried out, he will be the first member of the US military to be executed since 1961.

According to the Death Penalty Information Center, the 1961 execution was carried out by hanging. The apparent last known execution by a US military firing squad was one carried out “by musketry” in November 1945, the center reported.

articles.title: Navratri 2026: When does Sharad Navratri begin? Know date, significance, puja and rituals
articles.summary: Navratri is just around the corner, and for many people, this is when the festive season really starts.
articles.body: Navratri is just around the corner, and for many people, this is when the festive season really starts.The mornings can be quite different during these nine days. There may be a diya burning in the puja room, prayers being said at home and a vrat meal being planned for later in the day. And then, come evening, things can get a lot more lively. Garba music, dandiya nights and people dressed in their festive best become part of the scene.Sharad Navratri, also known as Shardiya Navratri, is dedicated to Goddess Durga and her nine forms. It is observed for nine days, after which Vijayadashami, or Dussehra, is celebrated on the tenth day.If you're observing Navratri this year, or simply want to know when the celebrations begin, here's a look at the dates, rituals and traditions associated with it.When does Navratri start in 2026?Sharad Navratri begins on Sunday, October 11, 2026, and ends on October 19. Dussehra will be celebrated on October 20.The first day of Navratri falls on Shukla Pratipada in the Hindu month of Ashwin.In New Delhi, the Pratipada tithi begins at 9:19 pm on October 10 and ends at 9:30 pm on October 11.October 11 is also when devotees following the tradition perform Ghatasthapana, or Kalash Sthapana. It marks the start of Navratri puja.Why is Navratri celebrated?The festival is closely associated with the story of Goddess Durga and Mahishasura.According to Hindu mythology, Durga fought Mahishasura and defeated him after a long battle. Her victory is seen as the victory of good over evil, which is why the story holds such an important place in Navratri celebrations.The celebrations then move towards Vijayadashami. The tenth day is also linked to Lord Rama's victory over Ravana and is observed as Dussehra in many parts of the country.But there isn't really one way to celebrate Navratri.In Gujarat, the nights are filled with garba and dandiya. In West Bengal, Durga Puja becomes the centre of attention, with large pandals and community celebrations. In many North Indian homes, people observe vrat, perform puja and prepare for Kanya Puja.The traditions may look different, but Goddess Durga remains at the centre.What is Ghatasthapana?For families performing Navratri puja at home, Ghatasthapana is one of the first important rituals.It is also known as Kalash Sthapana. A kalash is placed in the puja area and worshipped through the nine days. Barley seeds are often sown beside it and allowed to grow during Navratri.The puja doesn't have to mean setting up an elaborate arrangement. Families may light a diya, offer flowers and fruits, prepare bhog and recite prayers or mantras.Some devotees also read the Durga Saptashati, or Devi Mahatmya, during the nine days.The muhurat for Ghatasthapana depends on where you live. So if you're planning to perform it at home, check the local panchang for the timing in your city rather than following a time meant for another location.Is fasting compulsory during Navratri?No.Fasting is an important part of Navratri for many devotees, but everyone doesn't follow the same routine.Some people keep a vrat throughout the nine days. Some fast only on certain days. Others have one meal during the day and avoid particular foods.And then there's the familiar Navratri food.Sabudana, kuttu, sama rice, makhana, potatoes, fruits and dairy products are commonly eaten during a vrat. Sendha namak is generally used instead of regular salt.But even this can vary. Families often have their own vrat recipes and food habits, while regional traditions can be different too.So don't be surprised if one person's Navratri thali looks nothing like another person's.Those who are fasting generally follow the rules they have grown up with or those followed in their family tradition.What are the nine forms of Goddess Durga?Each of the nine days is dedicated to a different form of Goddess Durga.They are Shailputri, Brahmacharini, Chandraghanta, Kushmanda, Skandamata, Katyayani, Kalaratri, Mahagauri and Siddhidatri.Devotees worship the form associated with each day and offer prayers, flowers, bhog and other items as part of the daily puja.The final days of Navratri are particularly significant in many homes. Durga Ashtami and Maha Navami are observed with special prayers, and some families also perform Homa and other rituals.What is Kanya Puja?Kanya Puja is another Navratri tradition, especially common in North India.You may have seen young girls dressed up and invited into homes during the festival. They are worshipped as manifestations of the Goddess.In many households, their feet are washed before they are served food. They may also be given a small gift or some money after the meal.The food prepared for them generally follows the family's Navratri food traditions.Even the day of Kanya Puja can differ. Some families perform it on Ashtami, while others do it on Navami.Why do people celebrate garba during Navratri?And then there is garba, which has become almost inseparable from Navratri celebrations in many parts of India.In Gujarat, the evenings can stretch late into the night, with people gathering in large numbers to dance. Traditional outfits, colourful jewellery and dandiya sticks are all part of the scene.The same festive energy can now be seen in cities far beyond Gujarat too. Large garba and dandiya events are held across India, attracting people who come to dance, meet friends and simply enjoy the festive mood.For some people, garba is a major part of their Navratri experience. For others, it isn't part of their celebrations at all.A family may spend the morning doing puja and the rest of the day observing a vrat. Another may visit a temple and then head out for garba in the evening. Some may keep the celebrations completely at home and focus on Ashtami, Navami and Kanya Puja.That's the thing about Navratri. The same festival can look quite different depending on the family, region and traditions you grew up with.There are homes where the nine days are quiet and prayerful. There are others where the evenings are all about music, dancing and getting dressed up.Even the food isn't the same everywhere.But underneath all these differences is the same central belief. Navratri honours Goddess Durga and celebrates the victory of good over evil.Once the nine days end on October 19, Vijayadashami will be celebrated on October 20.For some, that will mean Dussehra puja and celebrations. For others, it will simply be the next stop in what is usually a very busy festive season.Get the latest movie news, reviews, and celebrity updates. Download the TOI App.

articles.title: Ofcom investigates Meta over Instagram Instants feature
articles.summary: The regulator said Instagram had not fully assessed risks posed by its Instants feature prior to launching it.
articles.body:
Ofcom is investigating whether Meta breached its duties under the UK's online safety laws with the launch of its "Instants" feature on Instagram.

The tool - allowing users to take and share an instant image with close friends, that disappears once viewed - was launched on Meta's photo-sharing app in May as "a new way to share photos in the moment".

But the regulator said the social media giant had not properly assessed risks posed by the feature prior to launching it - something it is required to do under the UK's Online Safety Act (OSA).

A Meta spokesperson said in a statement that it "takes its regulatory obligations under the Online Safety Act seriously".

"We conducted a risk analysis and briefed Ofcom about this feature on a number of occasions before launching it," they said.

"We will of course co-operate with Ofcom during this investigation."

Ofcom said its probe would examine whether Meta breached OSA duties by not carrying out "a suitable and sufficient illegal content risk assessment and children's risk assessment before the launch of Instants".

Under the UK's sweeping online safety rules, platforms including Meta must carry out and update risk assessments to comply with a range of duties, including to tackle illegal content.

They must also show how they prevent children permitted to use their services from encountering content deemed harmful for them.

This spans material relating to pornography, or promoting self-harm or suicide - as "priority primary content" - alongside things like abusive, hateful or bullying content.

"Our online safety laws are clear – significant changes to platforms must be risk assessed before they're launched," said Ofcom enforcement director George Lusty.

"This is a vital step that tech firms must take to protect their users," he added.

"You wouldn't launch a new car without testing it properly, and it's the same for online services."

What the Online Safety Act is - and how to keep children safe online

Instants rolled out to the app's users in May as a way for people to share spontaneous images - something that was once what the app was all about.

Images shared with Instants can be viewed by those who have been selected as "close friends" by a user, or those who they follow and are followed back by.

Meta says the feature has a range of built-in protections, including for younger users with Teen Accounts, including preventing screenshots, reshares or forwarding of Instants.

But disappearing messages and images have been singled out previously as posing particular risks for child or teen users of some apps .

"Safety by design must be built in, not bolted on, and today's investigation shows we'll take action where we have concerns that providers are failing to comply," Lusty added.

Ofcom's decision to launch an investigation into the platform comes as Meta, TikTok and X also seek to challenge the regulator's enforcement of the OSA through judicial review .

All three companies have appeared in court this week, arguing they should not need to provide so much information in response to Ofcom's formal requests.

Meta has separately also argued Ofcom should not be able to levy fines for breaches based on its global annual revenue.

It also contends that its messaging and image-sharing apps should not have to face additional requirements under the OSA, such as tackling paid-for fraud ads.

articles.title: Palestine weekly: Olive harvest opens under assault
articles.summary: Israeli settlers and forces beat Palestinians, set property on fire and steal crops across the occupied West Bank.
articles.body:
While olive picking season is yet to officially begin, Palestinians began early efforts to reach their groves this week – and so did the Israeli settlers.

Across the occupied West Bank, harvesters were beaten, trees were burned, crops and tools were stolen, and Israeli soldiers closed land to its owners.

Meanwhile, in Gaza, Israeli strikes continued to ignore a year-old “ceasefire” as the territory’s humanitarian and medical systems slid further towards collapse, with winter around the corner.

The week’s violence suggests a bloody olive harvest to come in the occupied West Bank. On October 3 in Jabal Qamas, between the towns of Osarin and Beita south of Nablus, settlers from the illegal Mevaser Shalom outpost attacked a family of harvesters. The pogrom left one man, Hussam Adily, in critical condition, and injured his brother and mother, according to Israeli activist Jonathan Pollack and Arabic-language media reports.

The settlers then entered Osarin, ransacking a home and smashing cars. Although the Israeli military opened an investigation, it said the attackers had fled before soldiers arrived, The Times of Israel reported.

Similar pogroms on Palestinian olive pickers occurred across the north and centre of the West Bank, including in the villages of Rantis, Sebastia, Beit Imrin, Deir Sharaf, Aqraba, az-Zawiya, Ramin and Arrabuna. Farmers were pepper-sprayed, run over, or struck with sticks and fists, with several requiring hospital treatment, according to the Palestinian news agency Wafa and local field reports.

In Beita’s Jabal al-Arma, Israeli settlers opened fire on pickers and forces lobbed tear gas directly at them.

With attacks also came theft: Settlers made off with harvested olives, ladders and tarps in Sinjil – where thefts have been a near-daily occurrence for more than a week, according to Sinjil resident Ayed Jafry – as well as in Rafat, Kafr Ra’i, Faqqua and elsewhere, according to Wafa.

Trees were targeted, too. Near Abu Dis, settlers torched roughly 55 olive trees, along with a family’s freshly picked harvest, according to Wafa. Elsewhere, settlers drove their flocks through Palestinian-owned groves, ruining crops in villages including Burqa, al-Mughayyir and Beit Duqqu, according to local field reports.

Where settlers were not blocking the harvest, soldiers often were. Israeli forces turned farmers away from their own land in Deir Istiya, Farkha, Haris, az-Zawiya and Silwan, confiscating identification cards and, in some cases, tools, according to Wafa.

In Beita, the Israeli army halted a harvest after settlers showed up. The incident was the fourth such shutdown that weekend, Haaretz reported, in an area beyond the army’s jurisdiction. Soldiers forced out international volunteers accompanying Palestinians at gunpoint and assaulted journalists covering the attack.

Beyond the olive groves, two Palestinians were shot dead in separate incidents involving settlers and Israeli forces within a day of each other. Mashhour Yassin, 51, was shot dead on October 1 as settlers stormed homes in Yasouf, east of Salfit. The Palestinian Foreign Ministry said that soldiers seized the keys to the ambulance carrying him and threw them away, delaying his evacuation.

Bahaa al-Natsheh, 19, was shot dead the next day near an illegal outpost outside Kobar, according to Wafa and other media reports. Israeli authorities are still withholding his body from his family.

Meanwhile, at a checkpoint east of Tulkarem, a 45-year-old Palestinian man died of cardiac arrest while being detained, according to the Palestinian Red Crescent.

After weeks of increasingly bellicose campaign rhetoric, Israeli institutions this week moved to check some of the governing coalition’s ambitions ahead of the October 27 election.

The Supreme Court unanimously reinstated the Arab-majority political lists – the United Arab List and the Joint List – to the ballot after an election commission voted to ban them. The court also voted 7-2 to reinstate far-left lawmaker Ofer Cassif. However, Sami Abu Shehadeh, the leader of Balad, a component party of the Joint List, withdrew his candidacy under pressure from the justices.

Separately, the election commission chairman fined National Security Minister Itamar Ben-Gvir for using his access to a Hamas prisoner for a campaign video, Israeli media reported.

Israel President Isaac Herzog said this week that Israeli politicians “have not done everything” they could to rein in settler pogroms – remarks that followed Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu’s dismissal of a mass settler attack on Jalud as the work of a “small number” of rioters, The Times of Israel reported.

Haaretz reported that the administration of US President Donald Trump is weighing sanctions against Israeli military units and a blacklist of officers over the pogroms, though any such measures are reportedly being held back until after both Israel’s election in October and the US midterms in November.

The United Kingdom, meanwhile, confirmed that it suspended or rejected more than 80 arms export licences to Israel since 2024, while continuing to supply components that feed into the international F-35 programme, a global defence partnership led by Lockheed Martin. Israel said the UK must close its consulate in occupied East Jerusalem by October 8.

Gaza: Killings persist under ‘ceasefire’

In Gaza, daily Israeli strikes continued to defy the year-old “ceasefire”. The Gaza Health Ministry’s toll since the so-called truce rose from 1,422 killed on September 29 to 1,460 by October 5. This brings the cumulative death toll since October 2023 to 74,243, after 181 previously unverified deaths were added this week.

Five people, including a mother and daughter from Gaza’s small Christian community, were killed when an Israeli strike hit the al-Asala building in Gaza City on October 3, an attack Israeli media said was targeting a Hamas official.

Six people were killed when a drone hit a passenger van in Tal al-Hawa on September 30, among them Ammar al-Sharafi, the brother of Al Jazeera correspondent Momin Alshrafi. A man was killed when his tent in al-Mawasi was struck on October 1.

On October 4, a six-year-old girl died after reportedly being shot by Israeli troops in Deir el-Balah, according to Wafa. A Palestinian journalist, Muhammad al-Najjar, was killed on September 30, becoming the 263rd reporter killed since Israel’s genocidal war began, according to Gaza’s Government Media Office.

Israel also continued to demolish damaged buildings in eastern Gaza City. Satellite analysis put the number of damaged structures across Gaza at roughly 200,000.

Meanwhile, hundreds of Palestinians attended a mass funeral for 105 people recovered from the rubble of several buildings flattened in October 2023.

articles.title: ‘Hitting the right nail’: Refugee rescue group defiant as Greece targets it
articles.summary: Aegean Boat Report founder Tommy Olsen insists he is defending the rule of law, as Greece opens trial against him.
articles.body:
Athens, Greece – To Greek authorities, he is the nefarious Norwegian mastermind of an international criminal organisation “operationally structured to commit repeated crimes”, which he secretly controls from his hometown of Tromso, north of the Arctic Circle.

To thousands of distressed asylum seekers on the Aegean, he is a hero who may have saved their lives by publicly alerting search and rescue authorities who might rather not have known of their whereabouts.

A Greek court will open trial proceedings on Tuesday against Tommy Olsen to decide who is right.

Olsen is the creator of Aegean Boat Report, an independent monitor of distressed vessels in the Aegean. When contacted, he alerts the Greek or Turkish asylum service and coastguard, depending on whose jurisdiction the refugees find themselves in.

The public prosecutor on the island of Kos, in the east Aegean, has accused Olsen of conspiring to smuggle refugees into Greece and to conceal them from authorities.

Olsen won’t be at the Kos court because Norwegian authorities thought the evidence against him too flimsy to grant extradition.

“They looked at what the Greek authorities described I had done, and they said, ‘There’s nothing illegal here. It’s actually protected activities,’” Olsen told Al Jazeera.

“When I inform Greek authorities of asylum seekers in their territory, on land, and give them their location, their names, and everything, that, supposedly, should be a good thing… But this the Greek authorities see as facilitating,” Olsen said.

The case is important far beyond the fate of Olsen, 54, who could face up to 20 years in prison if convicted.

Human rights organisations see it as Greece’s latest attempt to silence independent monitors of human rights abuses, for which the country has previously been convicted at the European Court of Human Rights (ECHR).

“The ECHR asked us to confirm certain testimonies that featured in cases before it, and since then, those decisions have condemned Greece for pushbacks,” said Maria Gavouneli, head of the Greek National Committee for Human Rights, the country’s top independent human rights authority.

Pushbacks are illegal turnarounds of potential asylum seekers. Under the Geneva Convention of 1951, signatories, including Greece, are obliged to provide an asylum hearing to anyone who requests one.

Aegean Boat Report is one of a group of organisations which provide verified evidence for ECHR cases.

“We’ve asked NGOs in the field … to provide information about pushbacks. This is not hearsay. This is a signed witness statement that can stand up in court. We record these and we can help the witness go to the prosecutor,” Gavouneli told Al Jazeera.

Evidence provided by Aegean Boat Report has also helped shed light on at least two dozen instances of improper practices employed by the Hellenic Coastguard.

Last month, the Council of Europe , Europe’s principal human rights body, said retraining of Greek law enforcement officers and other measures “do not yet appear adequate to comprehensively address the ‘systematic practice of “pushbacks”‘ identified by the [ECHR], while serious concerns continue to be raised in this regard by a large number of different sources”.

Ultimately, Greece can face the suspension of European Union funding if it fails to provide “genuine and effective access to international protection procedures”.

That, said Olsen’s lawyer, is why Aegean Boat Report’s work is undesirable from the perspective of Greek authorities.

“The whole logic here is judicial harassment. They harass the organisations and humanitarians to get them away from the border so there can’t be any record of irregular or illegal coastguard practices,” Zacharias Kesses, the managing partner of Athens Legal Firm, told Al Jazeera.

Greek governments have long tried to prove that certain aid groups help to smuggle people into Greece.

In the last eight years, prosecutors have shut down two organisations by arresting their members and charging them with trafficking and espionage.

But in January, all 30 members of Emergency Response Centre International, a Greek search and rescue group, were acquitted of charges similar to Olsen’s. Sarah Mardini, a Syrian Olympic swimmer, was one of their members.

Smuggling charges against Mare Liberum, a German search and rescue group, were also shelved for lack of evidence in 2024.

Still, both organisations were shut down.

“They force you to stop doing what you’re doing and spend money to clear your name. It took Sarah Mardini eight years to be acquitted, with all the help she was receiving,” said Kesses, who has represented all three groups.

Despite the fact that there has never been a smuggling conviction, the suspicion persists in the minds of Greek officials.

Last February, the government passed a law that cuts off public funding to an entire aid group if any one of its members is merely accused of a felony.

Defending the bill in parliament, Minister of Migration Thanos Plevris said aid groups that receive funding cannot justify the use of volunteers.

“If you receive money, you cannot have volunteers. Your people get paid legally from government money and European Union money. They’re not volunteers,” Plevris said. “If they’re not getting paid, they’re using their access to rejected asylum seekers in camps. I don’t want them to say, ‘Don’t worry, meet me here at night and I’ll help you get to Athens.’”

Even though Greece doesn’t control any of Olsen’s funding, it has cut it off. Fearing reputational damage, his sponsors have ended support for Aegean Boat Report.

“The bills for one year for the lawyers is perhaps 10 annual budgets for Aegean Boat Report,” he said. Two weeks ago, he sold his car.

“I’m sitting with the invoices for 19,000 euros ($21,000), without any ability to pay them.”

Then there is personal cost. Olsen, a former kindergarten teacher who left his job to become a full-time aid coordinator on the island of Lesvos during the 2015-16 refugee crisis, hasn’t been on holiday with his family for years because he devoted all his time to refugees. Four of his five children have grown up and left home during that time.

“I feel really guilty for putting them through this, because I have done this with open eyes,” he said. “I would take responsibility for this, but I also have to take responsibility … for the collateral damage around me. And my family has been this collateral damage.”

Kesses believed this case would be dismissed or end in acquittal, like the others before it. Unlike them, it may not succeed in silencing Olsen. Aegean Boat Report still bears witness to the distress of asylum seekers on the high seas.

“The attacks from the Greek authorities give me a sense that I’m doing the right thing,” he said. “I’m hitting a nail that hurts… The more they act up, the more they try to get me, the more I understand that I’m hitting the right nail.”

In 1923, when the refugees coming from Turkiye were Greeks fleeing the burning of Smyrna, another Norwegian, Fridtjof Nansen, engineered the world’s first population exchange between the two countries, probably saving hundreds of thousands of lives.

Although he does not draw a parallel with Nansen, Olsen also sees his life as devoted to a greater cause.

“I’m defending the rule of law,” he said, “and defending human rights. It doesn’t concern a small group of people coming into Greek islands. It concerns all of us. It’s something that we pass on to our children.”

articles.title: Fear and disruption for Ukraine's rail passengers as Russia escalates drone attacks
articles.summary: Ukrainians travelling by train are increasingly caught in the crosshairs of Russia's attacks.
articles.body:
Ukraine's railways have kept the country running since Russia's full-scale invasion in 2022. But attacks are intensifying, with more than half of all strikes on locomotives since then occurring this year alone, according to the state-owned operator.

Yuliia Ponomarenko, 27, a marketing specialist from Kharkiv, found her journey to Warsaw last month suddenly interrupted just short of the Ukraine-Poland frontier.

"The border guards started running around and shouting "Run! Get out of the carriages! There's shelling!"

A Russian drone had just hit a locomotive near the same border , and a special train carrying former British Prime Minister Boris Johnson and other European dignitaries, had passed through minutes before.

Passengers on Yuliia's train were kept waiting for six hours while the fire up ahead was put out and the line cleared, she says: "We were really lucky that we were delayed a little and it wasn't our train."

She is among an increasing number of Ukrainian passengers facing disruption and long delays, as air raid alerts trigger emergency evacuations far from the battlegrounds of the east.

In September alone, 5,831 trains had to be evacuated due to Russian drone attacks, state owned railway operator Ukrzaliznytsia told AFP news agency on Monday. This meant on average each day, 205 trains were stopped.

It appears to be part of a wider assault on Ukraine's infrastructure, with two bridges attacked in Kyiv in the past few days and passengers of a metro train caught up in one of the strikes.

Seventeen-year-old Anastasiia Ryvbalchenko has also experienced a narrow escape.

She and her fellow passengers were forced to leave their train at 4am, towards the end of a long of a journey from Odesa to Kirovohrad on 16 September.

"On my way to Odesa, there had been a lot of evacuations and now on my way back it was happening again," she says. "I was already thinking that if there was another evacuation, I just couldn't take it any more."

An hour and a half later, as passengers waited in the dark, a drone struck nearby.

"There was an extremely loud explosion and everyone started running into the woods," she said.

It is not clear what the target was, and in this case the train was not damaged, but with further explosions lighting up the night sky, Anastasiia decided not to linger, continuing her journey on foot before being picked up by her parents.

"I'm not going to travel by train anymore," she says.

Anastassia's journey was more dramatic than most, but delays – some brief, others that last for hours – are now commonplace.

Since Russian drones first started attacking moving passenger trains towards the end of 2025, the routine for passengers has become increasingly familiar: leave the train, scroll Telegram channels for updates on drone and missile launches, send messages to warn friends and family that the train is delayed.

For a railway company proud of its record for punctuality, this year's disrupted schedule is posing a major challenge.

"We used to say that that during times of war we performed better than some railways in Europe in regular times,"the head of rail operator Ukrzaliznytsia, Oleksandr Pertsovskyi, told us.

"But now the life of our passengers and crew members is the utmost priority."

Russia's defence ministry denies targeting Ukrainian civilians and says its attacks on railways target the infrastructure used to transport military personnel and equipment.

The dangers are very real. Attacks on Ukrzaliznytsia's rolling stock and stations have risen sharply.

Of the 521 locomotives hit since the start of Russia's full-scale invasion, almost 60% have been this year, according to statistics released by the company. Overall attacks on railway facilities have risen from 1,206 in 2025 to 1,700 so far this year.

"The latest wave of escalation and real war with railways is becoming extremely intense," said Pertsovskyi.

"It's a combination of the deadly force of their shahed drones and precision that they achieve with cameras and mesh networks so they can hit moving targets."

According to Pertsovskyi, some of Russia's most recent drones are equipped with AI tools and image recognition. Ukraine is understandably cagey about how it goes about confronting this increasingly sophisticated threat, but electronic methods to disrupt the drones' connectivity are high on the list.

"Unfortunately, this is always a cat-and-mouse game," he said.

Watch: Why a Russian strike on train near Ukraine-Poland border could mark an escalation

Ukraine's prized steel industry left in ruins by Russian missile campaign

A four-minute warning isn't enough: Russia's new relentless missile tactics exhaust Kyiv residents

We were given rare access to an underground bunker in Kyiv, dubbed – appropriately enough – the "Iron Command Centre", where railway staff monitor threats in real time.

On one huge video screen, colour-coded passenger and freight trains could be seen making their way along the arteries of Ukraine's vast railway network.

We watched as a red icon representing a drone appeared to loiter over Kyiv, practically above our heads at one point.

Each drone had a 100km (62-mile) circle around it. Any passenger trains inside the circle would already have been evacuated, with customers not allowed to reboard until the train was outside the circle and the drone was still moving away.

"Our mission is not to let our train or our crew members be in that immediate attack area," Pertsovskyi said.

The company's precautions appear to have kept casualties low. Its figures for 2026 show that eight company employees have been killed, six of them when a ballistic missile struck a locomotive depot in Kyiv.

During our visit to Iron Command, another air raid siren sounded in Kyiv. The city's main railway station, we were told, was being evacuated.

On a later visit to the busy station, we found passengers waiting outside the main entrance or sheltering in underground passageways. Over the tannoy came news of steady stream of delays.

Everyone knows the coming months could be among the most difficult yet.

With winter not far off, Ukrzaliznytsia is already figuring out how to deal with evacuations when the outside temperature can reach -20C or below and snow is lying heavy on the ground.

Along with international donors, the company is preparing winter evacuation packs, mobile shelters and bus services in areas where evacuations become too frequent.

"We might be a slightly different railway, a reinvented railway," Pertsovskyi said. "But we'll keep connecting the country, no matter what, be it winter, be it summer, no matter how hard the enemy hits us."

articles.title: A 103-year-old World War II veteran has been tending the same basement bar in Maryland since 1963; after 63 years behind the counter, Irv Koch still opens when the first customer arrives
articles.summary: At 103, Irvin E Koch has spent more than six decades serving drinks from the basement of his own home in Pasadena, Maryland.
articles.body: At 103, Irvin E Koch has spent more than six decades serving drinks from the basement of his own home in Pasadena, Maryland. The World War II veteran has been behind the bar since 1963, and even now, there is no fixed time for the working day to begin.“The hours are very simple,” Koch, widely known as Irv, told The Washington Post. “When the first one gets here, that’s when it opens up,” he said. Closing time is just as flexible. The bar shuts when the customers leave or when Irv gets tired.The place is officially called Club Sunset Knoll, but it is better known as Irv’s Basement Bar. Located inside the waterfront house that Irv bought in 1963, the cash-only tavern has changed little over the decades. Its lights remain dim, drinks are inexpensive, a jukebox plays music and an old Smith Corona cash register still sits behind the counter.Irv has changed little in another respect- he still enjoys talking to customers and delivering one-liners that have been polished over decades. Asked recently whether he was the oldest bartender in the world, he replied, “Don’t ask me. I haven’t been around the world yet.” By several unofficial accounts, he is indeed believed to be the world’s oldest bartender.A bar that came with the houseIrv’s journey behind the counter was not the result of a long-held plan to enter the bar business. Born in 1923, he grew up poor in a south Baltimore neighbourhood, much of his childhood falling during the Great Depression. As a teenager, he joined the US Navy and served in the Philippines during World War II. His younger brother, Harry, later followed him into the armed forces.After the war, Irv worked as a builder for Sears and later as a plumber alongside Harry. His career changed when he bought the Pasadena property in 1963.The house had been built in 1912 as a summer home for a prominent Baltimore meatpacking family and was later converted into an inn. By the time Irv bought it, the property already had a functioning bar in its basement. “This was up for sale. We needed a house, so we bought the house - and guess what? The bar came with it,” Irv said.Instead of ignoring the unexpected addition to his new home, Irv decided to make it his livelihood. He never returned to another job. “Well, I was gifted it, so I took it. When I was born and all, everything was pennies, nickels and dimes. Now it’s twenties, fifties, hundreds. So that’s why I opened up the bar. For the money!” he said.His stepgrandson, Jason Cook, however, believes there is more to Irv’s decision to keep going. The bar makes enough money for Irv to live on, but Cook said his stepgrandfather also enjoys meeting and talking to people.“He loves the interaction, socializing with people. “He likes the attention, too. It definitely seems to keep him alive,” Cook said.Little has changed insideWalking into Irv’s Basement Bar means entering a place that has largely resisted the changes outside it. Messages written by visitors cover walls, ceiling tiles, chairs and other surfaces. Customers have left their names and notes across the bar over the years. Its card tables are worn, the pool table still takes quarters and the old cash register remains in use.Police department patches from across the US are displayed inside, while a large banner featuring Irv’s face reads- “Drinking where the sun don’t shine.”One of the bar’s most unusual features is the collection of bras hanging from the ceiling. Many have names written on them by the women who left them there. Irv remembers the first woman to do so as Amy. “She did it, I didn’t do it,” he said.There is no website, no phone number and no fixed schedule for people planning a visit. Irv also does not use a cellphone and dislikes credit cards, so customers need cash.Yet the lack of modern conveniences has become part of the attraction. While people once visited mainly for cheap beer, many now come because the bar offers an experience that feels removed from the digital age.A place people want to see while they canOn a recent evening, customers began arriving at around 6pm. Among them were regulars and a group of police officers. They ordered bottles of Coors Light while the jukebox offered music from performers including Buddy Holly and Dean Martin, along with country hits from 1960.Kathleen Hooper, 48, visited with her husband Robert to celebrate their 17th wedding anniversary. Although she had lived in the area for years, it was her first visit. “It’s almost like Ripley’s Believe It or Not meets ‘Coyote Ugly’ meets your neighbor,” she said.For Hooper, visiting had become something that needed to be done while Irv and his bar were still there. “This is a thing that people put on their bucket list. We just felt like we had to do it before we didn’t have the chance. Once it’s gone, it’s gone,” she said.Before leaving, she added her own message to a doorframe, joining thousands of visitors who have left their names behind over the years.Irv, meanwhile, has never seriously considered giving up the bar. Even after the deaths of his wife and his brother, he continued working. Cook, who now lives at the house with his wife and four children to help care for Irv, said his stepgrandfather never stopped.Asked whether he would make different choices if he could return to the past, Irv did not have many regrets. “If I could go backwards? There ain’t too much I would change,” he said.For now, Irv is looking forward to celebrating his 104th birthday in August. His basement bar continues to operate on the schedule it has followed for years and opens when the first customer turns up.You use AI every day. Now get your AI Quotient. Take the AIQ test.

articles.title: Iran turns citizens into informants as chilling crackdown spreads beyond its borders
articles.summary: Iran's Alaj platform crowdsources diaspora surveillance via Telegram, with an official source confirming the system to Fox News Digital.
articles.body: Iran has promoted a new system encouraging citizens to report information about Iranians living abroad, effectively crowdsourcing surveillance of the diaspora through a website and messaging platforms including Telegram, according to Iranian media reports and an Iranian official source who confirmed the program to Fox News Digital. The platform, known as Alaj — Persian for "remedy" or "cure" — asks users to provide information on people overseas whom it accuses of acting against Iran’s national interests or security. Iran International reported that tips could be submitted through the Alaj website, a Telegram bot and Iran’s Bale messaging service. The outlet reported that Iranian state television and the Revolutionary Guard-affiliated Fars News Agency also promoted the initiative. An Iranian official source confirmed to Fox News Digital that Alaj and the Telegram chatbot were established as a new system through which certain individuals could report information about Iranians living abroad. The source said the website was subsequently taken down after the project drew significant criticism inside Iran. IRAN ALLEGEDLY USED SOCCER CLUBS TO SPY ON CITIZENS, OPPOSITION GROUP URGES FIFA BAN REGIME BEFORE WORLD CUP The website did go offline shortly after its public rollout, although the reason for its suspension remains disputed. Iran International reported that Alaj claimed to have identified and monitored 1,600 people, including roughly 600 identified through reports submitted by members of the public. Those numbers have not been independently verified. The platform published names and photographs of Iranians abroad and, in some cases, national identification numbers, dates of birth and fathers’ names, according to the outlet. For Iranian American journalist and foreign policy analyst Lisa Daftari, the most consequential element is not simply that Tehran is collecting information, but that it is asking Iranians to report on one another. "Even if it's just the perception that other Iranians can report you or can get you in trouble or that this app exists, it makes a lot of people fearful," Daftari told Fox News Digital. "You'll think twice before going to that next protest." 'KEEP A LOW PROFILE': STATE DEPARTMENT WARNS AMERICANS OVERSEAS THEY COULD BE TARGETED Daftari said the fear is particularly acute for members of the Iranian diaspora who still have relatives inside the country. "Now your face could be captured, you can get in trouble," she said. "If you have family in Iran, they can get into trouble." Daftari described the approach as a digital extension of a much older system of control, arguing that Iran’s clerical establishment has spent decades creating uncertainty over whether neighbors, colleagues or acquaintances might report one another to authorities. "Now the regime wants to take this show on the road and do that here, here in the West," Daftari said. "They want to intimidate people. And it works." SECRET SERVICE AWARE OF IRANIAN VIDEO THREAT TARGETING BARRON TRUMP, AGENCY SAYS Daftari said she has experienced that intimidation personally for years. "I've been followed, I've been hacked multiple times, I have been approached in person in LA, in New York, even at the airport," she told Fox News Digital. She said that after one major hacking incident compromised her social media accounts as well as her personal and professional email, she was contacted by her local FBI office and began working closely with agents. Daftari said hackers also obtained private photographs of her in a bikini while she was on vacation and sent them to her husband. "The message they want to send is very clear, that we know where you are, we can reach you," she said. "And obviously the point is to intimidate and silence those who speak out, who report, who speak the truth and talk about all the crimes of this regime." She said the effects extend beyond prominent journalists or activists. Years ago, while filming at a Los Angeles café where Iranian Americans were watching a World Cup game, Daftari said she saw people attempting to hide their faces from the camera out of fear that footage could reach Iran and expose relatives there to retaliation. The calculation, she said, illustrates why a system such as Alaj can have an impact even if a target never knows whether information about them has actually been submitted. IRAN’S PROXY WAR HAS CROSSED OCEANS AND IS NOW KNOCKING ON AMERICA’S DOOR The threat has also changed Daftari’s own behavior. She recalled being unable to stop thinking about security when the location of her father’s memorial service had to be announced publicly after his death. Daftari said she routinely considers where she parks, what details she shares online and security vulnerabilities at places she visits. "It does silence a lot of people, and it does change the freedom by which we think we can operate here in the United States, where we believe we have full freedom," Daftari said. "Their intimidation works," she added. "It works to a certain extent on each individual." Daftari said the broader campaign should also shape how Americans understand the confrontation with Tehran, arguing that the threat extends beyond Iran’s nuclear program. CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP "It's not just about nuclear weapons, it's about a deadly ideology that has made its way here to U.S. soil," she said. "We have to understand that."

articles.title: One million UK people who have never smoked are now vapers
articles.summary: Latest statistics also show, for the second year in a row, more over-16s vape than smoke.
articles.body:
More than a million people who say they have never smoked are now vapers, latest data for 2025 reveals - up from around 940,000 in 2024.

People aged 25-34 are vaping more than any others, overtaking 16 to 24-year-olds, with 16.4% using e-cigarettes daily or occasionally.

For the second year in a row, more over-16s in Great Britain are using vapes or e-cigarettes than smoking cigarettes, according to the Office for National Statistics (ONS).

Meanwhile, the number of smokers in the UK continues to fall to nearly one in 10 adults, or 4.9 million people, down from 5.3 million in 2024, with more over-16s now vaping than smoking at 5.4 million.

Experts say the popularity of cigarette smoking has decreased as the harmful effects of tobacco have encouraged many to quit.

Vaping is less harmful than smoking, although the long-term effects are not yet clear, says the NHS.

It says non-smokers and people aged 17 and under should never vape.

The ONS figures show the percentage of people who had never used an e-cigarette continued to decrease in 2025 (83.0%) compared with 2024 (83.4%).

Twenty-five to 34-year-olds are now more likely to use vapes than 16 to 24-year-olds.

David Mais, from the ONS, said vapers were getting older and that "may reflect existing users getting older, growing popularity among this age group, or a combination of both".

New legislation in the UK , taking affect in the new year, will permanently ban the legal sale of tobacco to anyone born on or after January 1, 2009 to create a "smoke-free" generation.

Hazel Cheeseman, from the charity Action on Smoking and Health, said the latest statics showed encouraging progress in cutting smoking rates.

She added: "Smoking has fallen enormously over recent decades, but it remains the biggest driver of preventable death in the UK. Now is the time to finish the job."

According to the ONS, men were more likely to smoke than women in 2025, similar to previous years.

And people aged 45-54 had the highest proportion of current smokers (12.4%).

Young adults aged 18 to 24 years have seen the largest drop in smoking among all age groups.

Of the people who currently smoked in 2025, half said they intended to quit. Some 7.2% of people reported having used an e-cigarette, up from 6.6% in 2024.

Kruti Shrotri from Cancer Research UK said: "While a continued fall in smoking rates is encouraging, tobacco remains the leading cause of cancer in the UK.

"Although we don't know the long-term risks of vaping, evidence so far shows that legal vapes are less harmful than tobacco and an effective tool to stop smoking."

The vaping data includes people aged 16 and over in Great Britain, while the smoking statistics cover adults in the whole of the UK.

articles.title: MrBeast breaks personal YouTube record as $1 million grocery store video hits 125 million views
articles.summary: MrBeast has broken his personal record for the most views a YouTube video has received in its first 24 hours.
articles.body: MrBeast has broken his personal record for the most views a YouTube video has received in its first 24 hours. His latest video, Eat Everything In A Grocery Store, Win $1,000,000, quickly became a huge hit after being uploaded on October 3. The video had more than 70 million views in its first day and has now reached around 125 million views. The challenge follows four contestants who spent more than six months living inside a grocery store while trying to clear millions of calories of food.MrBeast’s $1 million grocery store video breaks his YouTube recordMrBeast revealed that the new video was his “most viewed video ever in 24 hours.” He also said that more than 10,000 comments called it his best video yet.The video had already passed 70 million views during its first day. It has since continued to grow and has now crossed the 125 million-view mark.The video is more than an hour long, but viewers stayed for a large part of it. MrBeast said the upload had already collected more than one billion minutes of total watch time. The average viewer watched for more than 20 minutes.The challenge itself had started earlier in 2026. MrBeast bought an entire grocery store and asked contestants to live inside it. The original winner was supposed to receive $250,000 for being the last person to stay.After 67 days, four contestants were still inside the store. Instead of ending the challenge, MrBeast changed the rules. He offered to refill the store and increased the prize to $1 million if the four contestants could clear all the food.How did the contestants win $1 million after 202 days?The contestants had to deal with about 4.3 million calories of food. They did not have to eat everything themselves. MrBeast created different ways for them to reduce the amount of food.Guests were brought in to help eat some of the food. Some food was also donated through challenges. The goal was to make sure as little food as possible went to waste.After 202 days inside the grocery store, the contestants finally completed the challenge. That means they spent more than six and a half months living inside the store.Almost all of the 4.3 million calories were cleared. Only 6,614 calories were left as waste. The four contestants then won the $1 million prize.The huge response to the video has also made it another big moment for MrBeast on YouTube. Even after 17 years of making videos, he does not think he has reached his peak.“Even though I’ve been making content for 17 years now I still think my best days are ahead,” MrBeast said.The record-breaking views show that his large challenges continue to attract millions of viewers. With the video still gaining views, its final total could become even bigger.You use AI every day. Now get your AI Quotient. Take the AIQ test.

articles.title: ‘Very deep cuts to his head’: Dentist recalls crucial 45 minutes that helped save flydubai hero Captain Smit Machchhar
articles.summary: An Israel-based dentist who was among the passengers on flydubai Flight FZ1073 has recalled the frantic 45-minute effort to save Captain Smit Machchhar
articles.body: An Israel-based dentist who was among the passengers on flydubai Flight FZ1073 has recalled the frantic 45-minute effort to save Captain Smit Machchhar after he was attacked in the cockpit during the Dubai-Tel Aviv flight.Dr Shota Musaev to ABC News that he rushed towards the cockpit after hearing screams and found Machchhar seriously injured and bleeding.Musaev said Machchhar had deep cuts to his head and left hand. He used T-shirts to press against the wounds and asked cabin crew for ice.“He had very, very deep cuts and we needed many ice packets,” Musaev told The National.“But every time I opened the T-shirt to check the bleeding, it would bleed more. So I pressed not very hard and with ice. All through the 45 minutes I kept the pressure on.”Musaev also tried to keep the injured captain conscious, telling him, "Please don't sleep, we need you," asking how many children he had and their names, and repeating, "Don't be afraid, you will go back to your family, we are landing soon." Machchhar told Musaev he wanted to live and complained of severe pain. "Please help me. My God is with me. I want to live. I don't want to die here," he said.At one point, Machchhar's pulse dropped sharply. Musaev raised his feet and said his pulse recovered. When the captain's lips turned blue, Musaev told a steward, "We need to land quickly. He doesn't have much more time."He said he decided against giving Machchhar painkillers because of the heavy bleeding. "He was lying on his back and I hesitated to lift him because I didn't want re-bleeding," Musaev said. "It was dangerous to move him or give him medicines."Passengers turned rescuersMusaev was among the passengers who helped restrain the co-pilot after the attack, telling Ynet, "There were a few brave people there. We took control of the attacker and tied him up. Of course it was difficult, but we managed." The passengers used headphone cables to restrain his hands and legs as he continued struggling."I came to fight the attacker when I heard the screams. I didn't come to provide medical treatment, but after we tied him up, I treated the stabbed pilot," Musaev said. Two standby pilots then entered the cockpit with a passenger to help steady the aircraft, while other passengers remained alert in case there were further threats."We were at the plane exit, in front of the cockpit, and every time we scanned the area, we were worried there may be more terrorists on the plane," Musaev said. A group of passengers continued watching the cabin until the aircraft landed in Saudi Arabia.Passengers initially feared the aircraft was crashing after it rapidly lost altitude. "We thought we were going to die, 100%," Musaev told Ynet. "The plane lost an insane amount of altitude in half a minute." He added, "We saw the pilots and started screaming, 'Bring the pilots.' Then when one of them went into the cockpit and took control, we understood that we had survived."The aircraft diverted to Tabuk, where Machchhar was handed over to doctors.Musaev later learnt that the captain had survived and was out of danger, recalling that he told Machchhar, "Good luck my friend. Everything will be good." He added, "Smit saved our lives. Smit is a hero and I thank him for everything he did to save my family, all the passengers," before calling it karma: "He saved our lives and we saved his life."What happened on FZ1073Flight FZ1073 was flying from Dubai to Tel Aviv on September 30 with 174 passengers and crew on board when the co-pilot allegedly attacked Machchhar with a crash axe.UAE attorney general Hamad Al Shamsi has described the incident as an “attempted terrorist attack”. Authorities said the co-pilot tried to take control of the aircraft after attacking the captain.Despite his injuries, Machchhar managed to open the cockpit door, allowing passengers and crew to intervene.The Boeing 737 MAX 8 landed safely in Tabuk. Machchhar was treated in Saudi Arabia before being transferred to the UAE, where he is recovering.You use AI every day. Now get your AI Quotient. Take the AIQ test.

articles.title: Germany arrests former spy chief over treason and espionage allegations
articles.summary: Germany’s former foreign intelligence chief August Hanning was arrested on Tuesday on suspicion of treasonous espionage and passing sensitive information
articles.body: Germany’s former foreign intelligence chief August Hanning was arrested on Tuesday on suspicion of treasonous espionage and passing sensitive information to overseas intelligence services, the federal prosecutor’s office said.Hanning, 80, headed Germany’s Federal Intelligence Service, or BND, from December 1998 to November 2005. Prosecutors said he is “strongly suspected of treasonous espionage, spying out state secrets, attempted treason, and espionage.”A former aide, identified as Manfred D, was also arrested. He was detained in Steinfurt in western Germany, while Hanning was arrested in Bad Toelz-Wolfratshausen in southern Germany. Manfred D is suspected of aiding and abetting attempted treason and treasonous espionage.The prosecutor’s office did not identify the foreign intelligence service or services allegedly involved.According to prosecutors, Hanning and Manfred D agreed in spring 2010 that the former aide would continuously provide Hanning with intelligence from the BND “in exchange for remuneration”.Manfred D had served as Hanning’s chief of staff and later held the same position for several of Hanning’s successors between March 2012 and March 2026. Prosecutors said that role gave him access to confidential material.“The current findings suggest that, over the years, Manfred D provided Hanning with approximately 2,000 documents, many of which contained classified information to be used exclusively by the Federal Intelligence Service for internal purposes, particularly for executive intelligence briefings,” the prosecutor’s office said, according to AP.Prosecutors further alleged that “on one occasion, Hanning used classified intelligence ... to draft an analysis for an officer of a foreign intelligence service”, although investigators have not established whether the material reached its intended recipient.Hanning is also accused of being “in close contact with a representative of another foreign intelligence service, to whom he passed on political information, partially based on material provided by Manfred D, for several years”.German broadcaster ARD, citing security sources, reported that the material allegedly included information concerning Iran’s nuclear programme and the Russian army. Some of it was reportedly obtained from partner intelligence agencies abroad.Marc Henrichmann, chairman of the German parliament’s intelligence oversight committee, told AFP that Germany would “not tolerate the betrayal of secrets”.“Whoever allies themselves with the enemies of our liberal democracy will be found out,” Henrichmann said, adding that Hanning’s alleged conduct would represent “trampling his official duties underfoot”.The investigation reportedly emerged from a separate case involving Christina Block, a steakhouse chain heiress on trial over the alleged kidnapping of her children. Hanning’s property was searched in September 2025 as part of that investigation.Premises linked to both suspects were searched at several locations, including Berlin.You use AI every day.
