articles.title: Saudi Arabia says three wounded in attacks on airports near Yemen border
articles.summary: Saudi aviation authority reports severe injuries and damage following Houthi strikes on Jazan and Najran airports.
articles.body:
Saudi Arabia says three people have been wounded in attacks on two airports near the Yemen border.

King Abdullah bin Abdulaziz airport in Jazan and Najran airport were hit in the attacks on Monday evening, Saudi Arabia’s Civil Aviation Authority said in a statement on Tuesday.

“The attacks resulted in three minor injuries and material damage,” it said.

Yemen’s Houthis, an armed group also known as Ansar Allah (Arabic for Supporters of God), said late on Monday that their forces targeted sites across southern Saudi Arabia, including airports and military sites.

The attacks caused injuries of “varying severity” and material damage, and the injured have been taken to hospital, the Saudi civil aviation authority said.

“Specialised teams dealt with the attacks immediately upon their occurrence,” the authority said, adding that it will continue to assess the damage and is taking measures to protect passengers and staff.

Gulf Cooperation Council Secretary-General Jassim al-Budaiwi called attacks on airports and civilian facilities “a dangerous escalation”, and urged the international community to take a “firm stance against these attacks”.

Kuwait’s Ministry of Foreign Affairs also condemned the Iran-aligned group’s “continued brazen and disgraceful attacks” on Saudi Arabia, accusing it of targeting civilians and economic facilities.

The attacks on Saudi airports come amid an escalation in fighting in Yemen, where forces loyal to the internationally recognised government, backed by Saudi Arabia, are battling the Houthis.

The Saudi-led coalition in Yemen said early on Tuesday that it destroyed a ballistic missile launch platform in Yemen’s capital Sanaa, which the Houthis have controlled since 2014.

It also said it destroyed a storage facility in Saada that had 20 ballistic missiles, according to the official Saudi Press Agency.

The announcements came after forces aligned with Yemen’s internationally recognised government launched a counteroffensive to retake territory the Iran-aligned Houthis captured last month. The Yemeni government-aligned forces said they have retaken the port city of Mocha on the Red Sea and are now in control of the strategic Bab al-Mandeb strait.

The Saudi-led coalition has confirmed its participation in the Yemeni government offensive, saying 100 of its fighter jets are providing air support. Saudi naval forces have also launched an operation against the Houthis in Hodeidah governorate, the coalition said.

Fernando Carvajal, a former United Nations Security Council adviser on Yemen, told Al Jazeera that Mocha would be key to the next phase of clashes.

He said government forces will have to prove that they can hold on to the city, which is “surrounded by Houthis from all three sides”, before using it as a staging point.

Meanwhile, Turkiye, Pakistan and Saudi Arabia agreed to activate “deterrence measures” under a mutual defence pact and rapidly deploy forces to the Gulf kingdom to counter Houthi attacks.

“The committee agreed to activate collective deterrence measures, within the framework of the Alliance, in response to the attacks and all those responsible for them,” Khalid bin Salman, Saudi Arabia’s defence minister, said in a social media post.

He said the alliance had “reaffirmed the solidarity and unity of our countries, in confronting the heinous attacks against the Kingdom, and holy sites”.

Carvajal said it remains unclear what practical support they will provide. He said Pakistan might try to mediate between the warring sides, but that the Houthis would likely only want to talk to the Saudis, which would leave the Yemeni government excluded.

articles.body: Kentucky bourbon executive Wes Henderson lost his job earlier this month after family members accused him of using hidden cameras to record relatives and guests at his homes and a castle resort, according to reports. TKC Distilling, the parent company of The Kentucky Castle and True Story Whiskey, terminated Henderson as CEO Oct. 3. "It is our understanding that the complaint will be voluntarily dismissed. If that does not happen, he is prepared to vigorously defend himself." Family members alleged that they discovered concealed cameras during a June 2025 stay at Henderson’s vacation home near Melbourne, Florida. They said they removed about 15 cameras, including devices disguised as fire alarms. They also found cameras hidden in a fan, a clock, a speaker, charging blocks and outlet extenders. WEST VIRGINIA PRINCIPAL SUSPENDED AFTER RECORDING DEVICES FOUND IN GIRLS’ LOCKER ROOMS They also reportedly found a camera hidden in a bathroom air vent and footage showing Henderson positioning a camera in front of a bed. articles.title: India opposition leaders briefly arrested in protest against election chief
articles.summary: Protesters are demanding the resignation of Chief Election Commissioner Gyanesh Kumar.
articles.body:
Police have briefly arrested several opposition legislators in New Delhi for trying to breach barricades during a protest march to demand the resignation of ⁠the election chief over a controversial revision of voter lists.

Rahul Gandhi, a leader of the Congress party, was among the lawmakers detained in the Indian capital on Tuesday, but was released soon after, the AFP news agency and local media reported.

The march is the latest in a series of near-daily protests beginning last week led by student groups, opposition parties and India’s “Cockroach” youth movement.

The protesters are demanding the resignation of Chief Election Commissioner Gyanesh Kumar, accusing the polling body he oversees of manipulating voter registrations to benefit Prime Minister Narendra Modi’s ruling Bharatiya Janata Party.

“The election commission is a puppet in the ‌hands of the government,” Congress President Mallikarjun Kharge told reporters as the march began.

“After failing multiple times, Congress leaders have decided to establish anarchy in ⁠the country and attack institutions,” BJP spokesperson Sambit Patra told reporters before Tuesday’s protest.

Lawmakers carried placards, waved the national flag, and shouted slogans against Kumar during the march, roughly 1km (0.6 miles) long, to the Election Commission headquarters from parliament, through the centre of New Delhi.

India began its Special Intensive Revision of voter lists in Bihar last year before state elections. The exercise has since expanded to most states and federally administered territories.

Critics say the process requires documents that are confusing and difficult to obtain, risking the exclusion of millions of eligible voters. Election Commission data shows voter rolls could shrink by as much as 30 percent in some regions.

The Election Commission says the voter-roll revision is designed to remove duplicate, deceased or ineligible entries and maintain electoral integrity. On Friday, it directed its officials to register eligible voters inadvertently omitted from electoral rolls.

articles.title: 'UNRWA is Hamas,' Israeli attorney warns as explosive Oct 7 lawsuit rocks UN agency
articles.summary: The family of Yonatan Samerano, killed fleeing the Nova music festival on Oct. 7, is suing UNRWA after the Knesset stripped its diplomatic immunity.
articles.body: A legal battle between the family of an Oct. 7, 2023 attack victim and the United Nations Relief and Works Agency for Palestine Refugees in the Near East (UNRWA) has become a lightning rod for ongoing uncertainty about the agency’s future in the Gaza Strip. Israeli civil rights attorney and president of the Shurat HaDin Law Center, Nitsana Darshan-Leitner, told Fox News Digital that she filed a lawsuit in the District Court of Jerusalem on behalf of the family of 21-year-old Yonatan Samerano, who was murdered outside of Kibbutz Be’eri after fleeing the Nova music festival on Oct. 7, 2023. Samerano’s body was returned to his family after 625 days in captivity, during the final stage of hostage releases, Darshan-Leitner said. According to Darshan-Leitner, after Samerano was shot to death by terrorists, his body was picked up by UNRWA workers, placed in a UNRWA vehicle and kidnapped to Gaza. "Although the kidnapping was by UNRWA’s workers, UNRWA never revealed the place of the body, never cooperated with Israeli authorities to tell them where Yonatan Samerano was held and never admitted that it was done by its workers. And therefore we decided to sue UNRWA on behalf of the family." TRUMP BRINGS NEW HEAT TO CONTROVERSIAL UN AGENCY AS ALLEGED HAMAS TIES ENGULF SCORES OF EMPLOYEES The difficulty in bringing suit against UNRWA has been the diplomatic immunity the organization enjoys by virtue of the Charter of the United Nations and the Convention on the Privileges and Immunities of the United Nations. Darshan-Leitner said that the charter "specifically prohibits any act of violence, let alone terrorism" and that because "UNRWA was aiding and abetting terror organizations and participating in acts of terrorism, they can no longer enjoy the immunity granted by the treaty." The Israeli Knesset passed legislation in December stripping UNRWA of its diplomatic immunity, which allows the Israeli government to expropriate UNRWA properties within East Jerusalem. Due to UNRWA’s loss of immunity, the Samerano family is pursuing punitive damages of NIS 24 million (nearly $8 million) under Israel’s Compensation for Victims of Terrorism Law. When the deadline for UNRWA to file its defense in the case arrived last week, Darshan-Leitner said that the agency asked for a 45-day extension. UNRWA did not respond to requests for comment about the status of its immunity, or its response to the litigation it faces on behalf of Samerano’s family. US URGES DONORS TO ABANDON UNRWA FUNDING AS UN DEFENDS AGENCY'S MISSION Stéphane Dujarric, spokesperson to United Nations Secretary-General António Guterres, told Fox News Digital that Guterres has consistently "stated that the Knesset Law and its amendments are inconsistent with the status and international legal framework applicable to UNRWA. The source of UNRWA’s immunities is vested in the Charter of the United Nations and the Convention on the Privileges and Immunities of the United Nations, which remain applicable." While Guterres "has been very clear that any UNRWA personnel who has been demonstrated to have participated in the terror attack on Israel on Oct. 7 must be held accountable," he added that "Whenever we have been given information by the Israeli government on such individuals, we have acted." UNRWA’s role in the future of Gaza has been hotly contested in passing months. As the USAID Office of Inspector General and NGO Watch continue to turn up evidence of Hamas infiltration of UNRWA, Finland, Sweden and the U.S. have now fully stopped issuing funds to the organization. The Board of Peace, charged with the reconstruction of Gaza, has stated that UNRWA will have no role in the future of the Strip. However, The Associated Press reported on Sept. 25 that the Board of Peace members "have been more open to working with the U.N. agency for Palestine than it seems." Their article cited a Board of Peace official’s confirmation that "board members had met multiple times with UNRWA officials." The Board of Peace shot back on X, saying that its "policy as it relates to UNRWA’s involvement in Gaza is unchanged. We will only work with trusted partners who will deliver for the people of Gaza and contribute to a deradicalized Strip. UNRWA fails on those litmus tests." UN-BACKED DATA UNDERCUTS VIRAL GAZA FAMINE CLAIMS AS CHILD MALNUTRITION FALLS A U.S. official told Fox News Digital that "The evidence continues to mount that UNRWA has become a vehicle for instability, violence and radicalization, and it has no place in Gaza’s future humanitarian operations. At the same time, we are confident there are many capable and dedicated service providers in Gaza today who, following robust vetting and background checks, will meet the high standards required to deliver critical goods and services to the Palestinian people. We expect many will welcome the opportunity to continue that important work in partnership with credible NGOs, other U.N. entities or alongside the [National Committee for the Administration of Gaza.] Following an orderly wind-down, UNRWA itself will neither be essential nor necessary to accomplishing the work that lies ahead in Gaza." Guterres continues to stand behind the organization. In remarks he delivered at the Ministerial Meeting on UNRWA on Sept. 24, the U.N. leader stated that "UNRWA remains a critical stabilizing presence." UN CHIEF BACKS OFFICIAL WHO REPOSTED ANTI-ISRAEL ACTIVIST'S CLAIMS AMID CALLS FOR INVESTIGATION "For years now, UNRWA has been forced to operate under extraordinary pressure. I have repeatedly condemned in the strongest terms the appalling attacks by Hamas and other armed Palestinian groups against Israel on Oct. 7, 2023. Since then, UNRWA’s personnel in Gaza have endured terrible loss and hardship. Nearly 400 members of its workforce have been killed. Hundreds of its premises remain inaccessible, severely damaged, or utterly destroyed," Guterres said. Guterres also said that "a ceaseless political campaign has tried to manipulate public perceptions, undermine UNRWA’s ability to operate, and deny the rights of Palestine refugees." He called on U.N. Member States to "take immediate action" to politically and financially support the organization and protect its mandate. Darshan-Leitner said that allowing UNRWA to continue operations inside Gaza would be problematic. "UNRWA indoctrinated [Palestinian refugees] and let the terror organizations infiltrate their schools and education facilities." She added that UNRWA facilities "served Hamas as bases, as launchers, as missile storage places," which both "risk the life of the citizens in Gaza," and ensure that there will be collateral damage if Israel retaliates against attacks. So letting UNRWA take care of the humanitarian needs of the population in Gaza is a fatal mistake," Darshan-Leitner said.

articles.title: 'Dhappa': Cops tried to stop INDIA bloc's march to EC; Rahul Gandhi pulled a surprise
articles.summary: NEW DELHI: The protest route was planned, and the police were prepared. But then came a “Rahul twist” in the planned script.
articles.body: NEW DELHI: The protest route was planned, and the police were prepared. But then came a “Rahul twist” in the planned script.The INDIA bloc's protest march on Tuesday was supposed to begin at Parliament House and end at the Election Commission headquarters, where opposition MPs planned to demand Chief Election Commissioner Gyanesh Kumar's resignation over alleged irregularities in the Special Intensive Revision (SIR) of electoral rolls.As expected, central Delhi was heavily barricaded. Police and paramilitary personnel were deployed along the route, traffic diversions were put in place and access to the Election Commission office was restricted.But midway through the protest, leader of opposition in Lok Sabha Rahul Gandhi and his sister, Wayanad MP Priyanka Gandhi Vadra, pulled a surprise on the cops.As police started detaining INDIA bloc MPs and moving them into buses after stopping the march, Rahul and Priyanka did not remain on the road waiting to be taken away.Priyanka first boarded a bus parked near the building and Rahul prepared to follow her.But then suddenly they changed their course and walked into the nearby Akashvani Bhawan premises, taking their protest away from the heavily secured route to a new location and catching the cops off guard.The two later sat under a tree near Gate No. 4 as staff of the broadcasting house rushed outside to watch the unfolding drama.Outside, the Congress leaders began gathering at the reception entrance, seeking to join the Gandhi siblings inside. Some of them KC Venugopal, Pawan Khera, Imran Pratapgarhi and Srinivas BV subsequently joined the sit-in protest, while others climbed the boundary wall and raised slogans.Later, Congress did not miss the opportunity to flaunt the surprise “detour” and shared a video of the move with a playful 'dhappa' caption. The video showed the protesters changing route just when police appeared to have brought the march under control.This is not the first time Rahul Gandhi has pulled a surprise on the cops during a protest.On July 21, a day after police action against students and youth during a protest at Jantar Mantar against NEET paper leak, Rahul and a group of Congress MPs unexpectedly reached near Prime Minister Narendra Modi's residence and began an impromptu sit-in. The move was a surprise not just for the cops but also many Congress leaders who were only told that they were gathering to wish birthday wishes to party chief Mallikarjun Kharge. That protest ended only after police physically removed Rahul and other leaders from outside the PM’s house.This time, Rahul changed his method. He announced a protest plan and started on the planned course. But instead of waiting for police to arrest him, he and Priyanka quickly moved the demonstration to another location.Earlier in the day, Rahul climbed a police barricade and waved the national flag as INDIA bloc MPs attempted to move towards Nirvachan Sadan. Police eventually stopped the march, detained several leaders and began taking them away in buses.Congress leader Pawan Khera hit out at the security deployment that prevented opposition MPs from reaching the poll body to submit their memorandum. Rahul, too, questioned why opposition leaders were being prevented from meeting Election Commissioners."More than 300 opposition MPs marched from Parliament to the Election Commission today to meet the Election Commissioners. We represent crores of Indians. Why aren't the Election Commissioners meeting us? Why is the police stopping and threatening us?" Rahul said.The march was part of the INDIA bloc's wider campaign against the Election Commission over the SIR exercise. Opposition parties have accused the poll body of disenfranchising eligible voters and have demanded Gyanesh Kumar's resignation. The INDIA bloc has also sought the scrapping of the current SIR exercise and restoration of names it alleges were wrongly deleted from electoral rolls.The Election Commission has rejected the allegations."The ECI is a constitutional body that functions under the strict mandate of Article 324 of the Constitution, statutory rules and established institutional conventions. The Commission operates as a multi-member constitutional body. Written notes, observations, technical suggestions and internal checks-and-balances are standard, ongoing practices designed to ensure complete transparency, legal compliance and operational rigour. All actions of ECI have been in accordance of laws and instructions of the Commission," the EC had said in an official statement."Differing views and observations are a normal part of deliberation in any institution. They are a part of the decision-making process before a final decision is taken. Not only the three Commissioners, but every officer of the Commission is fully authorized to give his suggestions to the Commission for improving the electoral system," it said.The BJP, meanwhile, accused the opposition of attempting to undermine a constitutional institution. Party spokesperson Sambit Patra alleged that the Congress and its allies were trying to create "anarchy" and use the confrontation with the Election Commission to politically relaunch Rahul Gandhi."A sponsored attempt is being made by opposition parties, especially the Congress, as to how a change of power can be brought about in the country and Rahul Gandhi be made to sit in power just like that. For this, a blow to India's democracy and constitutional bodies is being hurled in a sponsored manner," Patra said.The protests are still not over.The march has now turned into a sit-in. Delhi Police and Rapid Action Force personnel are still stationed outside Akashvani Bhawan while the Congress leaders remain inside. It will be interesting to see how the cops handle this: Do they forcibly lift Rahul and other Congress leaders as they did in July? Or do they let the Congress leaders stay put while ensuring that the crowd does not swell?Get the latest India News and Live updates. Download the TOI app.

articles.title: Flydubai pilot planned 9/11-style attack, source tells NBC News
articles.summary: The pilot who tried to bring down an Israel-bound flight had been planning a 9/11-style attack, a Middle Eastern official has told NBC News.
articles.body: TEL AVIV — The pilot who allegedly tried to bring down an Israel-bound flight had been planning a 9/11-style attack by crashing into the country’s main airport in Tel Aviv, a Middle Eastern official has told NBC News. The pilot, identified by NBC News as Hamman al-Hamammi, told investigators Monday that he wanted to evade Israel’s defenses and crash into the Ben Gurion Airport or another building, said the official, who spoke on condition of anonymity because the person was not authorized to speak publicly. An Omani citizen, multiple sources from three agencies briefed on the investigation and a diplomat in the Middle East identified al-Hammami. Authorities have not officially released the identity. He is currently being questioned by investigators in the United Arab Emirates after he was transferred from Saudi Arabia. The flight from Dubai to Tel Aviv was diverted to an airport in Saudi Arabia, where it landed safely, after last week’s dramatic midair incident. Emirati authorities said Saturday that the pilot attacked his fellow pilot, Capt. Smit Machchhar, with a crash axe and attempted to take control of the aircraft’s flight controls. The jet which was carrying 174 mostly Israeli passengers then plummeted 14,000 feet in just 29 seconds, according to data from the aviation tracking service Flightradar24, causing panic onboard. Machchhar, an Indian national and a veteran pilot of 17 years, said in a call Friday with Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu that his fellow pilot told him he was going to pray, something he didn’t consider unusual as observant Muslims pray five times a day. A few minutes later, he said he felt a strong blow to the head. “Because of his initial blows, my vision was almost like nothing, and I was completely blurred out,” he added. “The next feeling that I had was that the aircraft was sharply going down.” A video of the call was released by Netanyahu’s office. Initially, Machchhar said, he thought there was “catastrophic damage to the aircraft,” but once the blows kept coming he “realized that it’s not the aircraft, it’s the other guy who was in the cockpit with me.” In a separate call with Indian Prime Minister Narendra Modi, also Friday, Machchhar said he managed to open the cockpit’s door on the second attempt, despite the blows raining down. “I gave everything that I had, and just went for the door and opened the door. And thankfully, people were waiting to pounce back,” he said. Focus has shifted onto the missed security signals ahead of the flight. Citing sources familiar with the matter, The Wall Street Journal reported Saturday that al-Hammami had “previously been banned from flying by Oman over concerns he had adopted radical ideological views.” It is unclear how a citizen of Oman, an Arab country with no diplomatic relations with Israel, was allowed to fly the plane carrying Israelis to Tel Aviv. According to Israeli law, airlines must provide information about passengers and crew members, including their names and nationalities, up to 48 hours before a flight. Netanyahu has called on the head of the National Security Council to appoint an examiner to review “all security aspects” of Israel’s civil aviation in the aftermath of the incident. Elsewhere, Vice President JD Vance underlined the concerns potential security failures. “That person should not have been flying an airline, and so we’re certainly looking at our procedures within the United States to make sure that people who are obviously flight risks are not getting behind the wheel of an airplane,” he told a reporter at Joint Base Andrews on Monday.

articles.title: Mapping where US bombers are based globally
articles.summary: The US has pulled its B-1 bombers from RAF Fairford amid Iran fears. Here’s where else they can fly from.
articles.body:
Over the course of Sunday, a dozen B-1B bombers took off from Royal Air Force (RAF) Fairford in western England and flew home to the United States. Their departure abruptly ended the base’s role as a launchpad for US strikes on Iran, which began on February 28.

The base, roughly 160km (100 miles) west of London, is the US Air Force’s only European airfield for heavy bombers and a key forward operating location for deployed bombers.

Over the past two weeks, six people were arrested on suspicion of “terrorism”. They were all released on bail.

US President Donald Trump said on Monday the bombers were moved because “there were some threats”, which he believed were linked to Iran. “So we moved them around a little bit, not very far,” he told reporters at the White House.

Hours earlier, US Secretary of State Marco Rubio played down any link to the alleged plot, saying it was “not unusual to see rotations happen” and that he had confidence in the security of US bases.

On September 27, police arrested five men on suspicion of plotting to plant explosives near Fairford in the United Kingdom. They were released on bail a day later.

Investigators found petrol but no explosive devices in their vans, though UK officials say the men remain under investigation . On Thursday, police arrested a 25-year-old UK-Iranian dual national in London on suspicion of plotting an attack on the airbase. He was also released on bail on October 3.

UK Prime Minister Andy Burnham suggested that “Iran played a part” in the alleged plot but declined to give details. Iran has denied any such scheme and summoned the UK ambassador in Tehran in protest at the arrests.

The US Air Force flies three types of bombers, with a fourth on the way.

The B-52 Stratofortress is the oldest. The B-52H model currently in service was built in the early 1960s. With a wingspan of 56 metres (185 feet), it is the largest US bomber and can carry about 31 tonnes of weapons, including nuclear bombs and cruise missiles.

The B-1B Lancer , which entered service in the mid-1980s, is the fastest of the three. It can reach 1.2 times the speed of sound and has a swing-wing that sweeps back for high-speed flight. It carries the largest conventional payload, about 34 tonnes, but no longer carries nuclear weapons. These were the aircraft that left Fairford.

The B-2 Spirit is a flying-wing stealth bomber designed to slip past air defences. Only 20 were built, of which 19 remain in service. It can carry both nuclear and conventional weapons, including the 13,600kg (30,000lb) “bunker buster” bomb used in US strikes on Iran’s nuclear sites in June 2025.

The B-21 Raider , a smaller stealth bomber, is still in flight testing, and it remains on track for delivery in 2027. Over the next decade and a half, the air force plans to replace the B-1B and B-2, leaving a future fleet of B-21s and upgraded B-52s.

All US bombers are permanently based in the US, at five main airbases:

B-52H: Barksdale Air Force Base in Louisiana and Minot Air Force Base in North Dakota

B-1B: Dyess Air Force Base in Texas and Ellsworth Air Force Base in South Dakota

B-2: Whiteman Air Force Base in Missouri

B-21: Due to arrive at Ellsworth in South Dakota in 2027

All of these bases have long, wide runways, typically exceeding 10,000 feet (3,048 metres).

That makes bomber runways about as long as those at a big international airport. What limits where bombers can operate is not tarmac but security, weapons storage and support.

For missions abroad, the US rotates bombers through a handful of forward bases. Other important overseas operating locations include Andersen Air Force Base in Guam and Diego Garcia in the Indian Ocean.

Beyond these, the air force sends small groups of bombers to allied airbases for a few weeks at a time, in what it calls Bomber Task Force deployments. Recent rotations have included B-52s at Moron in Spain, B-1Bs at Orland in Norway and Misawa in Japan, and B-52s at Tindal in northern Australia, which arrived in September.

The bombers can also go on a strike mission from the US with the help of aerial refuelling. Bomber missions during the US-Israel war on Iran lasted more than 30 hours there and back. Each group of three bombers needed six to nine tanker aircraft to refuel them along the way.

articles.title: In 1992, Mike and Dana Blevins bought a 300-acre Missouri property where cattle and heavy hunting had damaged the deer habitat; 34 years later, their restoration work has helped turn the land into a managed refuge for a thriving herd
articles.summary: Every time Mike and Dana Blevins take their side-by-side around their 300-acre property in Perryville, Missouri, they see something they once had to work
articles.body: Every time Mike and Dana Blevins take their side-by-side around their 300-acre property in Perryville, Missouri, they see something they once had to work hard to bring back: white-tailed deer. “We take the side-by-side out with our grandkids, and we will always see deer,” the couple told the Missouri Department of Conservation (MDC) in its September 2026 Missouri Conservationist feature. “Watching them year-round is a way we monitor the herd.” That routine is more than a family outing. It is also a quiet measure of how dramatically the property has changed since the Blevins bought it in 1992.A property where deer habitat had sufferedWhen the couple acquired the land, it was not being managed with a healthy deer population in mind. According to MDC, the previous owner allowed high hunting pressure and cattle to run in the woods, while the property lacked management aimed at supporting a healthy deer herd. The Blevins began changing that after purchasing the property.With recommendations from an MDC biologist, they introduced habitat-management practices designed to increase deer numbers. Over the following decades, the land became an example of how private landowners can work alongside wildlife officials to improve habitat and manage a local deer population. The transformation did not happen overnight. It unfolded over more than three decades, with the couple continually watching the animals and adjusting their approach. Today, seeing deer on the property has become an ordinary part of their lives.Missouri's remarkable deer comebackThe Blevins' experience is part of a much bigger Missouri conservation story. It is difficult to imagine today, but white-tailed deer once came close to disappearing from the state. MDC says widespread habitat destruction and unregulated hunting caused the population to collapse. By 1925, an estimated fewer than 400 deer remained in Missouri.Conservation efforts eventually reversed that decline. Protection, regulated hunting and habitat management helped the population recover dramatically. That recovery turned the white-tailed deer into one of Missouri's most familiar wild animals. MDC says nearly half a million people now pursue deer during hunting seasons, reflecting both the abundance of the species and its importance to the state's outdoor culture.But abundance also brings a management challenge. A healthy deer population requires suitable habitat, responsible hunting and continued monitoring, particularly as disease threatens herds in parts of the state.The new threat facing Missouri's deerFor the Blevins, habitat restoration is only one part of protecting the animals they have spent decades watching. Their focus has increasingly turned to chronic wasting disease, or CWD, a fatal and contagious disease affecting white-tailed deer and other members of the deer family. The disease can spread through contact between animals as well as through infectious proteins left in the environment. MDC has been testing Missouri deer for CWD for more than two decades. The disease was first detected in the state in 2010, after nearly 33,000 deer had been tested. Since then, the department has worked with hunters and landowners on efforts to keep infections under control.The Blevins became involved after learning about the disease. Mike Blevins said the couple previously owned an archery shop and wanted to ensure they could give customers accurate information about CWD. They have also participated in post-season targeted removal efforts, while continuing to harvest enough deer to feed their family and donate meat through Missouri's Share the Harvest programme.Missouri's deer recovery may be one of the state's major conservation successes, but officials warn that maintaining a healthy herd requires continued work. MDC says CWD remains relatively uncommon in much of Missouri, with less than 1% of tested deer statewide testing positive 15 years after the disease was detected. However, infection becomes harder to manage once it becomes well established in a population. For that reason, the department is shifting its approach toward more localised management, with hunters and landowners playing a central role during regular deer seasons.You use AI every day. articles.title: Guernsey GST will benefit the island, says Jersey tax expert
articles.summary: John Shenton says the introduction of GST will benefit the island, even if it is unpopular.
articles.body:
A Jersey tax consultant said Guernsey would benefit from introducing a 3% goods and services tax (GST) from 2029.

John Shenton, senior tax consultant at Grant Thornton, said people in Guernsey would "hate" the decision now, as Jersey people did ahead of its introduction there in 2008, but "after a while you get used to it".

He said he thought not exempting food from the tax had kept the overall rate lower - and if the exemption had been brought in the tax would now be closer to 10% instead of the 5% it had been since 2011.

His comments follow the States of Guernsey's decision to introduce a 3% GST from 2029 .

Shenton said Guernsey had "enormous problems" with its tax authority - with a 12-year backlog - which GST could help with.

He said: "Bringing in something which is relatively simple, relatively easy to administer, I think can only be a benefit to the people of Guernsey.

"They will hate it [GST], as did the people in Jersey, but I think after a while you get used to it."

Shenton said the tax had added about £1bn to Jersey's economy. This year, Revenue Jersey estimates the government will collect £132m in GST.

"If you took a billion pounds out of the Jersey economy over the last 18 years, then we would be in a much more sorry state than we are now," Shenton said.

He said Jersey would have had to increase other forms of tax such as social security or income tax.

Shenton described GST "as the best alternative" for Guernsey.

Goods and service exempt under the law include financial services, insurance, postal services, prescription medication, registered childcare and school fees, while buying, selling or renting accommodation and exports are among the goods and services zero-rated for GST.

Before and since its introduction moves have been made to exempt food from the tax.

Former politician Raluca Kovacs proposed to removing it from food in 2022 due to rising prices, but the move was defeated in the States.

She said: "I was hearing from people who were working hard and still struggling to put food on the table."

Kevin Lewis, who was part of the States of Jersey from 2005 until this year's election, voted against GST and voted for the tax to be taken off fruit and vegetables at the time.

He said: "I knew that we needed the money obviously, but I've got a problem with GST on food and I thought this is a slippery slope."

Lewis said he expected the tax to continue rising after it was increased from 3% to 5% in 2011.

Lewis said the main lesson Guernsey's government can learn from Jersey is to "pick a rate and stick to it".

He added: "People will never forgive you if it goes up too high."

articles.title: Atlanta robbery suspect allegedly steals police cruiser, crashes into tanker truck
articles.summary: Phelan Thorpe allegedly stole a marked Atlanta police cruiser and crashed it into a tanker truck on I-675 while wanted for a Midtown MARTA robbery.
articles.body: A man wanted in connection with the violent robbery of a woman near an Atlanta transit station was arrested Monday after allegedly stealing a marked police cruiser and crashing it into a tanker truck, authorities said. Atlanta police identified the suspect as 30-year-old Phelan Thorpe, who investigators say was wanted in connection with a Saturday afternoon robbery near the Midtown MARTA station. Thorpe was charged with robbery and simple battery in connection with the alleged attack, according to the Atlanta Police Department. Officers were dispatched shortly after 5:15 p.m. Monday to the 2000 block of Thomasville Drive SE after receiving a report that a wanted man was at the location and possibly armed, according to police. MAN FACING FEDERAL CHARGES AFTER ATLANTA TRAIN PASSENGER STABBED ABOUT 20 TIMES, FBI INVESTIGATING Officers located Thorpe and began investigating, but police said he managed to get into a marked Atlanta Police Department patrol vehicle parked outside and drive away. Thorpe allegedly drove the cruiser into neighboring Clayton County before crashing into a tanker truck on Interstate 675. SUSPECTED DUI DRIVER LEADS COPS ON WILD CHASE BEFORE DRAMATIC TAKEDOWN ON POPULAR CALIFORNIA BEACH He was taken into custody after the crash without further incident. Thorpe suffered minor, non-life-threatening injuries and was taken to a hospital, police said. No officers or other civilians were reported injured. Police had been looking for Thorpe in connection with an attack Saturday near 10th Street and West Peachtree Street in Midtown Atlanta. Officers responded at approximately 1:54 p.m. and found a woman who had been injured during an assault and robbery, according to police. FLORIDA MAN IN 'NO CHRIST NO LIFE' T-SHIRT CAUGHT ON VIDEO ALLEGEDLY ATTACKING, ROBBING WOMAN, 82, AT BUS STOP Investigators said a man had followed the woman from the Midtown MARTA station before confronting her and claiming he had a gun. Police said the suspect demanded the woman's purse and iPhone, leading to a physical struggle. The suspect allegedly punched the woman with a closed fist before taking her phone and driver's license, then fleeing the scene, according to police. The woman was transported to a hospital for evaluation. Surveillance video released by Atlanta police showed a man following the woman near a crosswalk before the confrontation. Police had initially asked the public for help identifying him. Atlanta police later identified Thorpe as the suspect wanted in connection with the robbery and said he was charged with robbery and simple battery. It was not immediately clear how Thorpe allegedly gained access to the patrol vehicle or whether police recovered a firearm. A police update Monday night did not identify any charges stemming from the alleged theft of the patrol vehicle or subsequent crash. articles.title: The India mood: Confidence in the country, anxiety about careers
articles.summary: Discover insights into the contrasting mood of India's populace, featuring high consumer confidence alongside concerns about unemployment and education. What does it mean for the nation's future?
articles.body: A sense of collective pride, and yet a feeling of individual disquiet. This is probably the most accurate description of the mood among India's more connected, urban-skewed population. There is confidence in the larger macroeconomic story, even as there is lingering uncertainty about the jobs market and an apparent weakening of the old assumption that education is a sure-shot route to upward mobility. Ipsos's September surveys capture that dilemma between hope and anxiety. India ranks first among 30 markets on consumer confidence but 16th on jobs, and unemployment is the issue Indian respondents worry about most.India's consumers are upbeat about the economy. In Ipsos's September 2026 Global Consumer Confidence Index, India scores 66.9, the highest among the 30 markets, compared with a global average of 48.4. Ipsos says its India sample is more urban, educated and/or affluent than the general population and hence the results should be read as reflecting the views of a more "connected" segment.India's Current Index, an indicator of how people rate present conditions, is 70.7, and its Investment Index is 73.2, both the highest among the 30 markets in the published survey. Its Expectations Index, at 66.4, ranks fourth, so respondents are also buoyant about the future.The contrast is particularly sharp against the world's major advanced economies. Among the G7, the US has the highest overall consumer-confidence score at 50.5, followed by Great Britain at 48.2 and Canada at 47.3. Italy scores 43.0, Germany 41.4, France 40.6 and Japan 39.4. India, at 66.9, is therefore 16.4 points above the best-performing G7 economy.Across the countries surveyed, India is the most confident market, followed by Sweden at 60.0 and Malaysia at 54.8. At the other end, Türkiye is lowest at 35.3, followed by Argentina at 37.8 and Japan at 39.4. The gap between India and Türkiye is more than 31 points. Only one number breaks the pattern. India's Jobs Index is 59.3, putting it in 16th spot. On current conditions and investment, India sits more than 30 points above the 30-country average. On jobs, its lead is just 1.6 points.Jobs top the worry listIn the September edition of Ipsos's What Worries the World survey, 47% of Indian respondents name unemployment among the three issues they find most worrying in the country, making it the most frequently cited concern in India. The global average is 29%. South Africa, Argentina, Singapore, Indonesia and Chile are the only countries with a higher share of respondents citing unemployment as a worry.Among the G7, unemployment is cited as a top concern by 28% in Canada and Italy, 20% in the US, 19% in Great Britain, 16% in France and 13% each in Germany and Japan, well below India's 47%. Across the 30 countries surveyed, concern is highest in South Africa, at 69%, and lowest in the Netherlands, at 6%.The same survey also finds strong optimism among Indian respondents. Seventy per cent say the country is heading in the right direction, against a global average of 38%. Only Singapore, at 80%, records a higher figure. Meanwhile, 79% describe the current economic situation in India as good, again compared with a global average of 38%.Here too India stands apart from the G7. The share saying their country is heading in the right direction is 44% in Canada, 36% in Japan, 28% in Great Britain, 27% in the US, 23% in Italy, 14% in Germany and 11% in France. Singapore does best on this measure at 80%, while France is at the bottom at 11%.The jobs concern, in other words, does not stem from general economic pessimism. The more connected Indians Ipsos surveys can be positive about the economy and still name unemployment as one of the country's most worrying problems.Ipsos switched its India consumer-confidence sample from a mixed methodology to online-only in April 2026, a break that the September report flags. Long-term comparisons therefore need caution.What the government data showDo the official numbers help explain this contrasting mood?Real GDP grew 7.8% year-on-year in the April-June quarter of 2026-27, according to MoSPI estimates. Private final consumption expenditure, the broad measure of household consumption, increased 7.1%, while gross fixed capital formation rose 11.9% at constant prices. Those numbers are broadly consistent with Ipsos's strong readings for current conditions and investment sentiment.The labour market data are more mixed. The government's monthly Periodic Labour Force Survey put India's unemployment rate for people aged 15 and above at 5.0% in August on the Current Weekly Status measure, marginally lower than 5.1% in July. But the improvement came from rural India. Rural unemployment fell from 4.5% to 4.1%, while the urban rate was almost unchanged, moving from 6.7% to 6.8%. The urban Worker Population Ratio was also 47.0%, unchanged from July and below 47.5% a year earlier.These figures are not directly comparable with Ipsos's Jobs Index. PLFS measures actual labour-market status; Ipsos measures perceptions of job security and the employment environment. There is another limitation to headline unemployment numbers. NITI Aayog has also highlighted job quality, informality and underemployment as labour-market concerns, dimensions that an unemployment rate alone cannot fully capture.Taken together, the data help explain how the seemingly contradictory findings can coexist.The classroom-to-career gapEducation is India's second-most cited concern, at 36%. That is the highest among the 30 countries, against a global country average of 13%. India's top two concerns, unemployment and education, are both closely tied to economic opportunity. The government's labour survey tracks one measure that spans both. In the latest PLFS annual report, covering 2025, 25.0% of people aged 15-29 were not in employment, education or training, or NEET. Among those aged 15-24, the share was 21.0%.The same report put the unemployment rate at 9.9% for 15-29-year-olds, 13.6% for urban youth and 6.5% for people with at least secondary education. NEET is not an unemployment measure: it also includes young people who are neither working nor studying but may not be looking for work. So for Indians, confidence in the economy, current conditions and investment is higher than in any other market. The Jobs Index is the exception, and the official data point to where some of the strain lies: among urban youth and the educated.That is the lived reality the surveys capture. The pride is collective: it is about where the country is heading. The disquiet surfaces when the conversation turns to jobs and education. With technology rapidly changing the nature of work, continuous learning and reskilling are becoming an economic necessity. But many workers and young people still lack the support, guidance and pathways needed to navigate that transition.The surveys offer a snapshot of that churn.Get the latest India News and Live updates. articles.title: Paramount-Warner Bros merger: Four ways the deal could affect you
articles.summary: The deal is expected to alter the entertainment and news industries but could it mean higher prices for consumers?
articles.body:
It has been months in the making but Paramount Skydance has finally completed its $110bn (£82.8bn) merger with Warner Bros Discovery.

The deal welds two legacy Hollywood powerhouses, uniting franchises like Harry Potter and Game of Thrones, into an entertainment behemoth named Skydance.

Yet behind this milestone lies strict rules about what the combined business can and cannot do - from how many films it must produce a year to the editorial independence of its newsroom.

Here are four ways this could affect you and the movies, TV and news you watch.

Warner Bros owns HBO Max, home to The Sopranos, House of the Dragon and Euphoria among others. Meanwhile, Paramount Skydance has Paramount+, which streams the likes of Yellowstone, Parks and Recreation and NCIS.

Combining HBO Max and Paramount+ into a single platform or bundle will likely squeeze subscribers' wallets over time.

While existing subscribers to both might enjoy short-term savings, analysts expect overall prices to rise as the combined giant seeks profitability .

The merged company, Skydance, carries a massive $80bn in debt from the deal, even as executives target $6bn in annual cost savings.

Mike Proulx, research director at Forrester Research, said viewers will undoubtedly get access to a bigger catalog.

But he told the BBC: "There's no way that a combined Paramount+ and HBO Max streaming service won't end up costing more for those who subscribe to only one of the services."

As part of a settlement deal with US states who had objected to the merger , Paramount Skydance has agreed to release a set number of films every year for the next five years.

For the first two years, that's 30 movies annually, and for the remaining period it has to release 32 films each year.

That's 156 movies in total - and the majority have to be "wide releases," meaning they must to be shown in cinemas.

The merged studio must also release at least four independent films each year.

If Skydance misses its movie quota, it could be forced to sell its 49% stake in Miramax – the studio co-founded by disgraced Hollywood mogul Harvey Weinstein.

Breanne Gilliam, a corporate lawyer at Maddin Hauser, said the film commitment is meaningful, even if it comes with an expiration date.

"Once those obligations expire, the company will have far more flexibility," she said.

"Temporary rules cannot permanently fix a structural market shift".

Once the five-year deal ends, Skydance could follow rivals like Disney and Netflix by prioritizing streaming over cinema.

As Disney's $71bn buyout of 21st Century Fox in 2019 proved, mega-deals can lead to fewer films in cinemas.

Before the acquisition, 20th Century Fox routinely released 12 to 17 movies annually in theatres, but under Disney that slate scaled down to just three to six a year.

For those working behind the scenes, the merger of two historic studios has been described as a "disaster" by those on the ground.

Actors and writers recently gathered at Paramount Studios in Los Angeles to oppose the deal, accusing regulators of failing to protect industry livelihoods.

Criminal Minds star Kirsten Vangsness told the BBC she was "heartbroken".

"It's people that make this city," she said. "It's people that make entertainment, it's the everyday creatives that this industry is built on - this is who it hurts."

A report by consultancy CVL Economics for LA County estimated the merger could eliminate roughly 4,500 direct film and TV jobs, while causing $1.26bn in lost wages over three years.

The blow could hit a region that has already lost roughly a third of its film and TV workforce, about 50,000 jobs, since 2022.

Syleecia Thompson, a business professor at National University, said that "it hits small businesses, vendors, caterers and local communities".

She warned that Hollywood may become less of a "single location" and more of a "dispersed network."

Although the settlement establishes a workforce fund to retrain displaced workers, lawyers note it does not block job cuts.

"Nothing in the settlement limits layoffs," attorney Gilliam added.

To address concerns over journalistic independence at CNN and CBS, the settlement creates a news editorial independence board that will be appointed directly by Paramount.

The $110bn deal brings two major US television news operations under a single corporate roof. Before the deal, Paramount owned CBS News, and Warner Bros. owned CNN.

Both networks have faced intense political pressure - CNN was one of a handful of news organisations banned from the White House by President Donald Trump - as well as leadership shifts amid broader industry consolidation.

Paramount chief executive David Ellison has asked CNN boss Mark Thompson - the former director general of the BBC - to remain at the helm after the takeover closes. CBS News's editor-in-chief Bari Weiss will remain in her role.

Yet as Paramount targets billions in cost cuts across the merged company, staff fear the consolidation will trigger significant job losses at CNN and CBS.

Beyond potential workforce reductions, media advocates and legal experts remain deeply skeptical about whether it can ensure newsroom freedom.

Seth Stern, chief of advocacy at Freedom of the Press Foundation, described the Paramount-appointed board as "worthless".

"The board creates the same First Amendment problems it claims to solve, the government meddling in news," Stern said.

Gilliam agrees paper promises mean little without real authority. "An oversight board only has as much power as the agreement gives it. Oversight without authority is just observation," she said.

articles.title: 'No meeting request received from any party': EC officials as Rahul, Priyanka refuse to leave 'protest site'
articles.summary: NEW DELHI: Election Commission on Tuesday said it had received no request from any political party seeking a meeting with its officials as standoff
articles.body: NEW DELHI: Election Commission on Tuesday said it had received no request from any political party seeking a meeting with its officials as standoff between the opposition and the poll panel intensified after Congress leaders Rahul Gandhi and Priyanka Gandhi Vadra refused to leave the protest site at Akashvani Bhawan premises.This comes as Rahul, Priyanka and other INDIA bloc leaders staged a protest near the Election Commission headquarters, demanding a meeting with the election commissioners to raise their allegations of "vote chori" and question Chief Election Commissioner Gyanesh Kumar.Responding to a query on whether INDIA bloc leaders had sought a meeting with the EC, poll panel officials said no such request had been received from any political party, according to news agency PTI.Rahul, Priyanka enter Akashvani BhawanThe INDIA bloc march began from Parliament Street and was headed towards the Election Commission headquarters, with opposition leaders demanding Gyanesh Kumar's resignation over alleged irregularities in the Special Intensive Revision (SIR) of electoral rolls.The march was stopped near the NITI Aayog office amid heavy security and barricading. Several opposition leaders, including Samajwadi Party chief Akhilesh Yadav and Trinamool Congress MPs Abhishek Banerjee and Derek O'Brien, were detained.The protest took an unexpected turn after police stopped the INDIA bloc march towards the poll panel's office. articles.title: Unknown Canaletto work could fetch £60k at Oxfordshire auction
articles.summary: The rare artwork is going under the hammer at Mallams auction house in Abingdon later this month.
articles.body:
A previously unknown work by the revered Italian artist Canaletto is set to go under the hammer.

The rare artwork, known as a capriccio, is estimated to fetch between £40,000 to £60,000 when it is sold by Mallams auction house in Abingdon, Oxfordshire, later this month.

Canaletto, whose real name was Giovanni Antonio Canal, was born in Venice in 1697 and went on to become a favourite of British art collectors.

Mallams said the artwork going under the hammer had been created by the 18th Century Venetian master with a pen, brown ink and a light grey wash on paper.

Art historian John Rolfe said the Canaletto work, Ruins of a Pavilion and an Arcade over the Water, was a "masterpiece".

He said it depicted "architectural splendours of the past in ruins" where "everyday life goes on amidst the shadows and sunlight".

"This drawing highlights a full range of the qualities that attracted contemporary collectors and inspired artists of future generations."

Canaletto was a member of the Venetian art school, and was best known across Europe for his cityscapes depicting Venice and London.

But in his home country, his capriccios - fanciful imaginary scenes, often showing classical ruins - were held in higher esteem, Mallams said.

It said the previously unrecorded work - which goes under the hammer on 21 October - corresponded with a Canaletto painting which was last sold at Christie's in 1995.

The work is thought to have been acquired by the Georgian composer and musician Charles Burney, and has been kept in the family since, the auction house said.

An inscription on the back of the work reads "a Present from Sig Canal d Canaletti", suggesting the artists had once given the work to someone as a gift.

Rupert Fogden, Mallams' director of fine art and pictures, said the auction house was "truly delighted to be entrusted" with the sale.

"Original paintings and drawings by Canaletto rarely come to auction, and we are expecting a significant amount of interest from both private collectors and institutions worldwide when it goes under the hammer this autumn," he added.

articles.title: 'Concern' as historic Devizes pond still a puddle months after heatwaves
articles.summary: The Crammer in Devizes has still not recovered despite rain throughout September.
articles.body:
There is "sadness" and "concern" as a much-loved 300-year-old pond remains dry months after this summer's extreme heat.

The Crammer in Devizes has no natural or artificial water source, making it reliant on rain and road runoff.

Residents describe it as the "focal point" of the Wilshire town and say they are "sad" and "concerned" the water has not returned despite rain throughout September.

Councillor Iain Wallis said filling the pond with artificial water would be expensive and unlikely when there are hosepipe bans .

Resident Lou Weaver said the much-loved pond is looking "very dire" and locals are waiting for more rain to refill it.

"It's always lovely to have the nice reflection of all the houses on the other side," she added.

Graeme Riley, who walks past it every day, said: "It's just sad really, it's the focal point of Devizes."

Wallis said dredging had been discussed, but is "really complicated".

"We can't really make it deeper because of the make-up at the bottom of the Crammer, you would just end up with more water running away.

"Unfortunately, because it's fed by road runoff, the mud that's in there, the silt is classed as hazardous waste. So the cost of dredging it would be probably in the low hundreds of thousands of pounds, and it's not a one-off cost," he said.

Dredging would be "appropriate" every couple of decades but cannot be something they do regularly, he added.

Resident Marion Kearley said she was concerned about wildlife. She spotted a flight of geese preparing to land in the pond before noticing they needed another spot.

"Very, very sad. I hope it will come back. I think it will but it'll take some time because it's obviously got to soak into what's there now, all the mud, before it starts filling. So I think we'll want a lot of rain," she added.

The latest data shows this summer was the hottest on record . Figures for the months of June, July and August show that the average mean temperature - which includes day and overnight temperatures - was 16.5C, the warmest on record in a dataset going back to 1884.

Drought was declared in all of Wales and more than two-thirds of England and wildfires caused devastation in parts of the country.

In a rapid attribution study - which looks at how much of a role climate change plays - the Met Office say the average temperature was made around 130 times more likely due to human-induced climate change.

articles.title: Badenoch's £10bn air defence plan points to growing concern over protecting UK's skies
articles.summary: The government and the Conservatives both agree the UK needs better air defences in an increasingly dangerous world.
articles.body:
America and Israel's war with Iran has shown that even the world's most sophisticated air defences can be overwhelmed by enemy missiles and drones, if fired in significant numbers.

Iran's have broken through the layered air defences of US military bases in the Middle-East causing significant damage.

Russia's war in Ukraine has also exposed the huge challenge of defending their own skies from large-scale attacks.

The government's Strategic Defence Review, published in 2025, explicitly warned of the threats to the UK – including ballistic and cruise missiles and drones – and highlighted the need for the UK to invest more in its air defences.

The Labour government is allocating up to £1bn to address it.

The Conservatives now say they will spend more - £10 bn - over a decade. Both parties agree that the UK needs layers of air defences.

Tories pledge £10bn for British anti-missile defence system

Currently the country has a number of systems to deal with short and medium-range threats – from drones to cruise missiles. But the armed forces still lack a weapons system to deal with long-range ballistic and hypersonic missiles.

And those don't come cheap. Each interceptor used by the US Patriot missile system costs about $4m (£3m).

Sophisticated air defences that can deal with a range of threats are expensive. The US Army alone wants to increase its budget for both missiles and interceptors by fourfold next year – to $36bn (£27.1bn).

Israel also spends a significant proportion of its $45bn (£33.9bn) annual military budget on air defences.

For the Conservatives there's also a presentation problem. Their original press release mentioned building a new air defence systems that would be "in essence, a British Iron Dome", referencing Israel's elaborate air defence system .

But any comparison of the challenge of defending Britain's skies with Israel's, about 10% the size of the UK, is naive.

Nor is the threat the same. Israel has regularly been targeted by drones and missiles over the past decade. The UK has not.

The Conservatives now suggest the phrase "Iron Dome" was just a shorthand for better air defences. But even the words "Britannia Shield" may be a misnomer.

It would be nigh on impossible for the UK to develop an air-defence system that could defend the whole country with such limited resources.

At best it could afford a system to protect some key strategic sites – including military bases. At present the UK doesn't even have that.

What are Israel's Iron Dome and other missile shields?

articles.title: Demonstrators clash with riot police in France as education protests mount
articles.summary: School blockades and clashes intensify in France as frustration rises over government education policy.
articles.body:
Police have fired tear gas at protesters blockading French high schools as tens of thousands of students and activists rally across France in a mounting wave of protests demanding government improvements to the education system.

Students in Marseille, Nantes and Lyon began demonstrations on Tuesday morning, with demonstrators holding aloft signs which read “they don’t really care about us” and “survive or study”.

In Strasbourg, Lyon and Rennes, the protests turned violent at times, with police firing tear gas and protesters lighting fires in the streets and hurling projectiles.

The protests started two weeks ago in Paris’s disadvantaged suburbs, lighting a blaze that has spread across the country. The government said that the movement has turned into urban violence and has deployed riot police to some rallies.

On Monday, a 15-year-old’s hand was blown off during clashes between high-schoolers and the police in northern France. The government said that around 200 to 250 protesters had thrown objects at the police.

A French newspaper, La Voix du Nord said that the teenager lost his hand and part of his arm after he picked a police grenade during the protest.

Nearly 2,000 high schools have been blockaded or closed for the day, according to the High School Students Union.

“When the answer is violence, it means democracy is no longer working,” said Hugo Vetzel, a recent high school graduate in Strasbourg preparing to attend France’s top universities. “There is such a gap between the elites and us.”

Al Jazeera’s Natacha Butler who was at a march in Paris said more groups are joining the demonstrations.

“We’re seeing people from various unions, like the farmers union, energy workers, teachers unions who’ve also said they’re going to come out in support of the students.” Butler said.

“Parents and teachers said they want to be here not just to support their children but to protect them as they are worried about troublemakers who may infiltrate the protests and excessive police force” Butler added.

Al Jazeera’s Rosie Birchard was at a demonstration in Lille and said students from neighbouring Belgium came to show support.

French Prime Minister Sebastien Lecornu has ordered ministers to address the students’ demands, including replacing underskilled teachers, making lunch breaks longer and changing the length of the school day.

Lecornu also said that the government will look into repairing old campuses, as he demanded ministers send in proposals by the end of October. But there are doubts about how quickly the government can respond.

“France is riddled with debt, France has a real budget crisis. Where would that money come from to put budget into public services” Al Jazeera’s Butler said.

France’s Ministry of Interior said that it has arrested 6,100 people since the beginning of the protests, the majority of them under the age of eighteen. The Ministry of Justice announced that over 1,800 will be prosecuted, including 1,483 minors.

During the protests, at least 215 teenagers have been wounded along with 715 police officers, according to Lecornu.

articles.title: US televangelist Jim Bakker, disgraced from sex scandal and fraud, dies at 86
articles.summary: US televangelist Jim Bakker co-founded The PTL Club with his then-wife Tammy Faye before being jailed for fraud and conspiracy.
articles.body:
US televangelist Jim Bakker, who built a multimillion-dollar media empire before being jailed for fraud and conspiracy, has died aged 86.

Bakker and his then-wife Tammy Faye founded a Christian television programme called The PTL Club in 1974, which at its peak attracted 13 million viewers per day.

The 86-year-old's death was announced on Monday by his second wife Lori Bakker, who described him as "a pioneer of Christian television".

By the late 80s, Bakker and Tammy Faye's empire began to fall apart after he became embroiled in a sex scandal and later convicted of mail and wire fraud. Tammy Faye, who divorced him in 1992, was never charged.

Bakker remarried in 1998, and alongside second wife Lori launched a new TV ministry in 2003.

Lori Bakker described her late husband as "my best friend, and the man I was honoured to walk beside through so many seasons of life and ministry".

However, Bakker's first program The PTL Club - short for 'Praise the Lord' or 'People That Love' - was what cemented his fame with his first wife Tammy Faye.

The couple built their empire with 2,000 employees and a 2,300-acre (930-hectare) Heritage USA theme park complex in Fort Mill, South Carolina.

The Bakkers had a famously opulent lifestyle, owning a private jet, multiple homes, luxury cars, jewellery and even an air-conditioned dog house.

In 1987, Bakker resigned from the PTL ministry after revelations of a 1980 sexual encounter with a former church secretary Jessica Hahn.

It later emerged Hanhn received a $265,000 payoff with ministry funds, resulting in Bakker being defrocked of his ministerial credentials and right to perform religious duties.

Hahn also accused Bakker of sexual assault, though the evangelist denied this, claiming the encounter had been consensual.

Bakker was then convicted in 1989 of 24 counts of mail and wire fraud and conspiracy in a scheme involving their Christian theme park, and served more than four years in prison.

Tammy Faye stayed with her husband throughout the trial but divorced him in 1992 while he was in prison. She died of cancer in 2007.

Following Bakker's release from prison in 1994, he wrote a book titled I Was Wrong and married his second wife Lori in 1998.

The couple began a TV ministry together in 2003 and in 2008 they began taping The Jim Bakker Show.

articles.title: Katie Price's ex, Kieran Hayler, told girl to 'take it to the grave'
articles.summary: The alleged victim is not part of Hayler or Price's extended families.
articles.body:
The former husband of Katie Price told a teenager after allegedly raping her that she should "take it to the grave", a court has heard.

Kieran Hayler, 39, is on trial at Lewes Crown Court accused of three counts of rape and one count of sexual assault in West Sussex in 2016, all of which he denies.

The complainant, who was 13 at the time of the alleged offences, wept during a police interview shown to jurors when she admitted lying to her mum about what happened because she "didn't want her to think I was disgusting".

She said: "I thought it was my fault for ages," adding that she told her mum Hayler had touched her but not that it was sex as she feared that "maybe I'd led him on".

The complainant told police that Hayler had called her two or three years after the alleged incidents had taken place.

She said: "He said something like 'you promise you won't tell anyone? What we had was special - you better take it to the grave', and that it might get me into trouble."

The complainant recalled him saying it might end badly for her, but that she had not felt frightened of him.

Asked by police how she felt following the three alleged rapes she said: "At the time I thought he really cares about me so he's not doing something horrible… because of the way he described it, he said it was a good thing."

The complainant remembered having "four showers a day after that" and said her mum recalled her "always washing" and changing her underwear "several times" a day.

She said: "I definitely remember thinking he's a lot older than me, is this something he should be doing?

"I remember crying and wondering if it should have been happening."

After the jury was shown the video of the police interview, the alleged victim gave evidence in person in court from behind a screen.

She was asked if she remembered anything else, and, speaking about the third incident, the complainant said Hayler had messaged her saying, "I love you, goodnight".

"I replied, 'I love you too'," she added.

In 2021, the complainant contacted the NSPCC charity which referred her to the police, prompting the investigation.

Hayler was first interviewed by police in January 2022 and denied any of the allegations took place and that anything sexual occurred.

He was married to media personality Price at the time of the alleged incidents, before the couple's relationship broke down in 2018 and they divorced in 2021.

Hayler suggested his ex-wife had "launched a campaign" against him when their marriage ended, and the allegations form part of this, the court heard.

The alleged victim is not part of Hayler or Price's extended families.

Price is expected to be a witness in the trial which is expected to last about a week.
